subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted, before discussing the budget proper, to make one observation regarding the Special War Revenue Act? I wish to call the attention of hon. members to section 20 which gives a prior lien to the government over other securities. The last paragraph of section 20 of the Special War Revenue Act, 1915, as amended, provides that the liability to the crown shall constitute a first charge on the assets of such person, firm or corporation, and shall rank for payment in priority to all other claims of whatsoever kind heretofore or hereafter arising save and except only the judicial costs, fees and lawful expenses of an assignee or other public officer charged with the administration or distribution of such assets.
In my opinion, Sir, this legislation is absolutely unjust to lenders in good faith on security. The practical difficulty of the existing law is that the creditor has no means of ascertaining whether the person to whom he lends his money is a debtor to the government. It is possible for the hypothecated immovable to become the asset of someone who is heavily indebted to the government, and if the property is brought to sheriff's sale the government will have a prior claim for Whatever might be due to them. To illustrate, let me mention a case in point. If a man lends $3,000 on a property on first mortgage, the value of the property being $4,000, and it is ascertained beforehand that the borrower is not indebted to the government, nobody can prevent this borrower from selling the property to another who is indebted to the government. The property is sold later on; the government has a prior claim and get, say, $3,000 due to them before the lender in good faith can get his money. I submit, Sir, that this section should be repealed, or provision made by which a government lien shall not prejudice the rights of creditors who have registered their claim previous to the property becoming the asset of the debtor. This would afford a means by which the creditor could protect himself.
I may add that this prior claim of the government does not exist in England. The creditor there who lends his money on property on which he takes a first mortgage ranks, if the property is sold, before the government in the matter of taxes, and so on. I hope that the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) will take note of this observation and remove this legislation, which in my opinion is most unjust and unfair to a creditor in good faith.
Now, Sir, I wish to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance on the excellent budget

that he has presented to the House this year.
I believe that in view of the difficult circumstances created by the late administration, the budget is a very good one. The Acting Minister of Finance has succeeded in balancing the budget and by keen business ability he has refunded maturing obligations and saved the country over $2,000,000 of interest a year. Our congratulations are due also to the High Commissioner for Canada in London, Mr. Larkin, in respect to the arrangements he has made regarding the loans to Greece and Roumania. He has some new securities on the revenues of these countries, especially on the wheat export, which will entitle us to hope that the taxpayers of Canada will be reimbursed some of the moneys that the late administration saw fit to scatter amongst its friends.
The best reason why, in my opinion, this budget is a sound and reasonable one is that it has failed to please the extreme wings of this House. It does not please the high protectionist and it also does not please the free trader. There is an old Latin saying, "in medio stat virtus." This budget reminds, me, Sir, of the attitude of Sir Wilfrid Laurier on racial and religious questions. The Tories of Ontario used to say that Sir Wilfrid wanted French and' Catholic domination, and at the same time the Tories of Quebec were stating that Sir Wilfrid was betraying his race and religion. Well, Sir, the principle that Sir Wilfrid Laurier did follow should apply to the fiscal policy, and I can see in this budget the embodiment of that principle. Our geographical situation is such that it is impossible to please everybody, and unless we make a firm determination to adopt a policy of give and take, a policy of conciliation, it will mean the disruption of confederation.
I wish to congratulate the government on the proposal they have made with respect to a tariff board. I believe that a tariff board will go a long way towards curing the ailments which beset us. I am not in favour of any iron-clad policy on tariff; I do not believe it will get us anywhere to say that we are high protectionists or to say that we are free traders. Every industry must be studied from the point of view of the interests of the consumer as well as those of the producer, and the duties should be increased or decreased accordingly. In my opinion certain duties should be increased and others should be decreased. I was in favour of the reciprocity-pact in 1911 with regard to agricultural products; I am still in favour of that policy, but I believe that until we get reciprocity in agricultural products with the United States we

should raise our tariff on those agricultural products to a point where it will be on a level with the high tariff of the United States on similar products.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Will the
hon. member permit a question? Would he also be in favour of reducing the duties on products coming into Canada where the United States duty is lower than ours, as in the case of boots and shoes, for instance?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Not on boots and shoes, but on agricultural products, absolutely. In my opinion free trade and high protection are not real policies. Free trade is a pious dream; high protection is a fit of hunger. I may add that everyone who has been studying the present evolution of fiscal matters must have noticed that the apostles of either extreme policy are becoming more scarce in this country. I call attention to our friends the Progressives. They came to this House, most of them, free traders, but I am sure that after having taken part in the affairs of this country, after having come in contact with all the diverse interests of this wide Dominion, they are not so strong on the policy of free trade to-day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I rise to my feet just to
challenge the statement the hon. gentleman has made that the majority of the Progressives came here as free traders.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
That is a very
fair challenge, but it does not prevent me from holding the opinion that if the hon. members of the Progressive party were ever returned to power, they would not dare to apply a free trade policy to this country. I may say the same thing about high protection. A few days ago we heard a very excellent speech by the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Putnam), in which he gave the House the opinion of a man who was a minister in the late administration, and who at that time endorsed the policy of protection, but who only a few months ago said that protection was not the proper policy for this country. I refer to Hon. Mr. McCurdy. And Mr. McCurdy's statement is such an interesting one that the House will permit me, although the hon. member for Colchester has already read it, to read it again. In a message to the press on the 5th of September last Mr. McCurdy said:
And first let me speak of the so-called "national'' policy, or system for protection, under and by virtue of -which it is certainly true that the manufacturers of Ontario and Quebec have fattened and grown rich, even although they are now passing through a lean period. But in what measure has this system of protection to industries alone helped us? It compels
The Budget-Mr. Archambault
Canadians, east and west, to buy the manufactured goods of Ontario and Quebec, but it still permits them to use American ports of entry and export for their goods, if so be they can wring a further profit thereby.
There, Sir, you have the opinion of a gentleman who formed a part of the late administration, who was supposed to endorse the policy of protection, but who is now coming out against that policy. This goes to show, Mr. Speaker, that the extremists on both sides are becoming more scarce in this country, and it is all for the benefit of the people.
If you look at the criticism of hon. members of the official opposition regarding this budget, you find that for the first time probably in the history of the Conservative party, their adherence to the policy of protection is not embodied in their amendment to the budget. What do you find in this amendment? You find that they contend that we should have more economy in this country. You find that they contend also that, we should have less taxation. I will refer later on to the increase in taxation and to economy, but I may say in passing that it is exhilarating to listen to their regrets and to notice the crocodile tears of the opposition regarding economy. There was only one instance pointed out by any member on the other side regarding economy. I challenge you, Mr. Speaker, to scan the speeches of the hon. members and find any real direct criticism, except in one instance, and this was given by the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) when he criticized the expenditure of the delegation to Wembley, and it was a pity to see the hon. gentleman the other night sitting in silence like a chastised child when the hon. member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Kyte) burst his bubble.
Sir, it is true that the duty of the opposition is to criticize. I admit that right away. But t'he opposition, if it has any desire to be useful to the country, if it has any desire to regain power, must also give to the House and the country valuable and constructive suggestions. There are no constructive suggestions in the amendment; there were no valuable suggestions in the speeches made by the hon. members of the opposition. In my opinion the amendment is simply a crazv-quilt of platitudes to cover the soreness and disappointment of the hon. members of the opposition. Reduction of taxation-who in this country does not wish to see taxation reduced? Economy-where is the hon. member who does not wish economy in the administration of affairs in this country? No, I repeat, Sir,

The Budget-Mr. Archambault
this amendment was made in a moment of disappointment and soreness by hon. gentlemen opposite, because the backbone of their political campaign has been broken by this budget. You will remember the criticisms which were offered last year. They were of two kinds: first, that the industries affected by the tariff would have to close their doors, and that there would be an adverse balance of trade against this country. The second criticism was, not that they were so much alarmed about the actual reductions then made, but they believed-indeed they were sure-that these small reductions on a few industries would surely lead to a general reduction this year. I heard these criticisms during the election of St. Antoine; I have heard them even on my radio since the election; I heard them when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) was tendered a banquet jointly with Armand Lavergne of Montreal. When we told these hon. gentlemen that the agricultural implement industries affected, like the Massey-Harris Company, and the International Harvester Company, were satisfied with the reduction of duties then made, they said: "Wait until next year. If you vote for the Liberal candidate in St. Antoine, you are giving the present government a mandate to go on, and to bring down more general reductions."
I may admit at the present moment, Mr Speaker, that they were partly justified by some-may I say, inconsiderate?-remarks of some of the members of the government. At the same time, that was the backbone of their policy, that was the backbone of their campaign: They were not afraid so much oi the actual reductions, but they were telling the people .that the government was going to make a general reduction in the tariff and that the industries of Canada would be crippled. What happened to those prophecies? The industries affected have made a better showing this year than they did before. The balance of trade, too, is in our favour. In 1924 we had a balance of exports over imports of $165,000,000; and in the first ten months of the year just closed we had a balance of export trade of $283,000,000. Therefore, those two prophecies have gone to the wastepaper basket. The third one has gone the same way. There are no wholesale reductions in the tariff this year.
So I was right, Mr. Speaker, when I stated that this budget has broken the backbone of the Conservative campaign. But they are not so easily daunted. Their backbone being broken they are sore, very sore indeed, naturally they have sought new devices and new alliances to try and fool the people once

more. I do not know very much about the campaign they are making in other provinces, but I know what is happening in the province of Quebec. Sir, we are offered in our province the most extraordinary spectacle and the most diverting entertainment for chasing the blues that we ever had. It is called "The great Conservative push" it reminds one of that little German putsch from Bavaria last year headed by the ponderous General Ludendorff followed by the Crown Prince to restore monarchy, which putsch with its combination of burlesque and slapstick comedy made the whole world rock with laughter. This great Conservative "putsch" came as far as Hull yesterday. The General Ludendorff of the "putsch" is the rotund Mr. Monty, who was a minister in the late cabinet but who could not find one Conservative constituency in Quebec that would elect him. The Krontzprintz of the party is none other than the celebrated Armand Lavergne, who has been hypnotized by the newly-discovered alluring charms and irresistible vamping powers of the right hon. leader of the opposition. They brought with them for protection the secretary of the Montreal Police Probe, Mr. J. H. Michaud; and occasionally the oratory of the party is elevated to the high planes or Gladstonian eloquence by Hon. C. C. Billantyne who has been nick-named in Montreal "Can't Come Back". Most of the publicity of that campaign is conducted in French in the official paper of the Tory organization called La Minerve. If the House will listen to me a few moments I think it would be greatly instructive to read just a few of the gems of this campaign; and after I have read them I am sure that hon. members will feel that I have not exaggerated in describing this new Conservative "putsch". Now, in the paper referred to on April 11, an account appeared of a lecture given in Montreal by a gentleman named Bousquet. Hon. Mr. Monty made a speech at that lecture which is headed in La Minerve "Sensational declaration of Hon. Mr. Monty". Listen to this-Mr. Monty is speaking:
In a great burst of eloquent words which made a great impression on his audience Mr. Monty violently denounced the secret pledge taken by the Liberal government with the English government to provide work for all the English immigrants, which means that if work is as scarce as it is now the Canadian worker will lose his job and be replaced by a " bloke
Listen to this one from La Minerve of 28th March, 1925, which is headed "Crime of High Treason." I translate:
When a Prime Minister of a country delivers, willingly or unwillingly, this country to the foreigner, and does that solely to remain in power it is called

The Budget-Mr. Archambault
by all the nations of the world a crime of high treason. Now the Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King is endeavouring to commit this crime; and if we do not take care, before five years all the provinces of the west from the west frontier of Ontario to the Rocky mountains will be annexed to the United States. Since three years the American citizens are invading the western provinces every year. It is by forty-five thousand and fifty thousand that they arrive annually to take hold of our land.
Listen to this gem:
If our* information is exact, and everything leads us to believe it is, Sir Loiner Gouin, backed by high personages like Mr. Holt, Mr. Beatty and others, is going to Europe simply to warn the King himself of what is going on here and prevent England from seeing one of the brightest gems of the British Crown being separated from the Crown.
Now, here is another published on February 28, 1925.

Were dt not for these blunders and this maladmistration, we would be paying $25,912.248 less in interest this year, $2,159,354 less per month, $498,427 less weekly, or $70,965 less daily every day including Sundays. I proceed to prove my contention.
I say, first, that through unnecessary war expenditure the national debt has been increased by the sum of $247,313,394. As my first witness, Mr. Speaker, I rely on a man of great reputation, a man who brought honour to his name and glory to his country during the war, a man who was in the best 141*

On September 11 last, speaking before the Citizens' Research Institute of Canada, he made a speech which startled the country, and which was never challenged. I had put on the order paper a resolution asking for an inquiry regarding these statements, but unfortunately my good friends the Progressives so clogged the order paper before they departed last session that it was impossible for my resolution to be reached.

If there is one thing more than another that has been responsible for the increase in our national debt and in our taxation, it is the expenditure due to the war. I do not know all about the expenditures of the war, but it is my opinion that it cost hundreds of millions of dollars more than it should have cost, or would have cost, if expert advice had always been available, and if such as was available had been listened to. I do not think I am exaggerating when I say that there were at least 100,000 men enlisted for the Canadian Expeditionary Force who never saw service in France, and who made no contribution to Canada's effort in the war. All these men were paid, fed, clothed, equipped, trained, cared for when sick, and transported. Many of them are still being cared for by the government, being in receipt of pensions or hospital treatment. I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that the average cost of these 100,000 men was $1,500 each, that had they not been enlisted $150,000,000 would have been saved. Furthermore, expert advice before the war and in the early months of the war condemned the Ross rifle. These experts said it was no good, and it was no good, yet strong pressure was exerted on Canadian units to continue its use, and even after it had been discarded by the first division other units were armed with it and forced to use it. Expert advice had condemned the harness supplied to Canadian troops as being unsuitable for use in war theatres, yet succeeding units were given this unsuitable harness as part of their equipment. Expert advice had condemned the Oliver equipment, yet Canadian units were supplied with it. There were other things also with which the Canadian troops were supplied which were scrapped in England before the units proceeded to France. I mention these flacts to illustrate the cost of neglecting to have available and to use expert advice.
Now, Sir Arthur Currie was the commander in chief of the Canadian army. If there is one man in the world who was in a position to judge these things, and who ds now in a position to tell the country that these expenditures were made through the blunders of the late administration, Sir Arthur Currie is that man.

Before leaving this matter I may say that similar statements to those of Sir Arthur Currie were made before-regarding the men, regarding the Oliver equipment, and regarding the Ross rifle. The statements were made in this House in 1917 by other gentlemen who are not here in this House, and we were accused of disloyalty for making these statements. I wish to bring to the attention of hon. gentlemen an editorial in the Montreal Gazette on the statement of Sir Arthur Currie, and I say without the slightest fear of contradiction that if in 1917 we had made speeches containing what is contained in the Montreal Gazette editorial of September 12, 1924, we would have been called disloyal by the members of the late administration. Here is the editorial:
The country is bound to be shocked and aroused by the startling charges of waste of effort and waste of money directed against our war governments by Sir Arthur Currie, our war general, last night.
Sir Arthur charged, first, that, "100,000 men were enlisted and sent to England who were of no use to us in the field."
This, it will be kept in mind, is the considered judgment of the man who commanded our armies in the field, and who thus knew exactly and by direct contact what men were of use and what men were not. His testimony is expert and practical testimony of unequalled weight. Yet he tells us soberly, six years after the war is over, that our authorities sent him 100,000 men who were of no use to the fighting forces in the field.
It is not too much to say that so grave and far-reaching a charge simply stuns. Sir Arthur calculates that each useless man cost the country $1,500. He is in a position to give us exact information on that subject. His estimate ought to be accurate. So we find no comfort in any hope that he may be wrong as we add up the astounding total and discover that this single category of blunders cost this nation $150,000,000.
But 'listen to this, and this is the part to which I referred a moment ago when I said that if we had uttered the statements mentioned in this article in 1917 we would have been called disloyal by the same group that ran the war.
Nor is this the whole story.
This is the Gazette speaking.
The withdrawal of 100,000 men from productive activity in Canada during whatever time they were in uniform, must have been of immense loss to the Dominion. Wartime industry was pressing every possible man into employment. Thousands who were rejected as unfit for the actual fighting, were gladly allowed to "do their bit " in the munition factories. Women were employed.
What a boon it would have been to have had the services at home of these 100,000 men who were fit enough to pass the examination and so must have been better than the unfit who did man the factories? Yet these men were taken away from useful employment, clothed, drilled and fed at the expense of the country, shipped to England at our cost and maintained there unproductively-a charge on the scanty food supplies of wartime Great Britain-and all because, as Sir Arthur says, expert advice was not taken or accepted. It was a terrible price to pay for ignoring the disinterested experts.
Here is the editorial of the Gazette.

I should like to extend to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) my congratulations on the manner of the presentation of his budget. Since coming into this House as a new member in the session of 1922 I have received at his hands nothing but the most courteous treatment, and I think it is only fair that I should so state on this occasion. As a member from the Maritime provinces, I should also like to join in the kindly references which have been made to the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). Those of us who come from the Maritimes, where we are few in number, have a feeling of distinct pride in the fact that the Maritime provinces have since confederation given to this country no less than three prime ministers and no less than three finance ministers, all men of exceptional merit and standing. That is an achievement of which in the short history of this young nation I think any small community may well be proud. Not the least among these distinguished men is the right bon. Minister of Finance whom I have the privilege and pleasure of referring to now. While we do not agree with him politically, while we think that many of the policies which he has enunciated and carried out in the past have been defective, yet we all recognize the fact that he has been a great public servant, and now when he is perhaps in the shadow of his lifetime I desire, as a Maritime province member, to accord him this mead of praise and appreciation.
While I can congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance on the manner of his budget speech, I regret that from the standpoint of the country it is not possible for me to offer him my congratulations on the matter of it. His budget has been criticized in various places and in various ways. Our friends on my immediate left are wont to call it a stand pat budget. It does not please them. I have searched in my mind for an apt term to apply to this budget, and I am of opinion that I can characterize it in no more fitting way than as a juggler's budget. When I was still a youth and before I took any great interest in public affaire, I well recollect how astounded I was at reading the reports of the budget speeches delivered in this House from 1896 to 1911 by the right hon. Minister of Finance. Knowing as I did that the Liberal party was pledged against the principle of high protection and to the policy of low tariff or free trade, I was puzzled to understand how it was possible that through all those years that party could -with any show of consistency, with any show of political decency and honour, pursue the course

which they did through fifteen long years. Having come into this House, however, and having watched the government and its supporters, I can understand the riddle. This party from first to last on the tariff question has adopted' the tactics of the juggler; on the one hand, it has sought to appease one element of public opinion by preaching free trade or low tariff wherever it thought it would be to their advantage to do so, and on the other, cheek by jowl, to extend to the manufacturers secret information that they had no cause to fear the Liberal party, with respect to high protection. Having listened to last year's budget and to this year's budget, last year's having been a gesture towards free trade, and this year's a gesture towards a stand pat policy, I now understand that it is the policy of this government, led by the Prime Minister, to adopt the same attitude that characterized the Liberal party during the many years when they were in office previous to 1911. You cap fool some of the people some of the time; you can fool all the people part of the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time, and the people of this country who believe in a tariff policy are beginning to find out just what the Liberal party stand for.
I think I can see the fine Italian hand of the Prime Minister in this budget. Last year we had a budget which in its material effects was a forward step in the direction of low tariff or free trade; so much so was it that it pleased a large majority of gentlemen immediately to my left and caused a considerable number of high protectionists in the Liberal party across the way to vote against it. It was of such a character that it caused the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who sits for the county of Argenteuil in the protectionist province of Quebec, to characterize it as the "death knell of protection" and to call down upon his humble head the execrations of many of his most ardent supporters in that county-in fact, to bring forth a demand for his resignation. The Minister of the Interior is still proclaiming that this government is a free trade or low tariff government. But he is doing it now at very low breath after having listened to this budget speech, and without any very great degree of sincerity or of conviction that as a result of this budget and what it foreshadows there will be any very material change in the tariff of this country.
Hon. gentlemen who sit to my left have by moving an amendment expressed disapproval of this budget, and if they represent public opinion in the communities from which they come they will stand by the wouldbe resolu-

I do not understand why some hon. gentlemen camouflage themselves any longer-we all know who they are in this chamber. Was it because of the fierce opposition to that proposal which arose in the Canadian west, as offered by their representatives here, or was it because it was one of those ill-conceived and ill-digested proposals that the government has brought down on more than one occasion? Perhaps we will know a little later just what the reason was that that child was stifled before it was actually bora. There is one thing it will do, however:	It will give some hon. gentlemen
to my left an excuse, or an opportunity, we will say, to support the budget. I venture to say that at least a dozen of them will support it; probably more than that, and this will serve as an excuse for doing so.
The most disconcerting phase of this budget, to my mind, is that in none of the proposals is there any relief for the tax-ridden people of this country. If there is one thing that is agitating the public mind at the present time more than another it is the burden of federal taxation-yes, and of provincial and municipal taxtion-which the people are labouring under. Unless there be some relief in this direction, especially with reference to the income tax, there will be an emigration of capital from Canada. This country lies for 3,000 miles along the border of the United States and anybody who has studied the fundamentals of taxation or of political economy knows that a country situated such as ours is should not have appreciably higher taxation than its neighbours to the south. Just so long as there is a marked disparity between the income tax in Canada and the income tax in the United States, just so long will there be an efflux from Canada to the south, where the taxation is lower. If hon. gentlemen have any doubt about it, let them obtain from any trust company the calculations as to the difference between the income taxation in Canada and that in the United States. Let me give a concrete illustration. I have in mind a gentleman living in New Brunswick who for years spent his winters in Florida. Recently he came to the conclusion that 'because of the decrease, or the promise of decrease, in taxation in the United States it would be much better for him to become a permanent resident of the state of Florida than to remain in New Brunswick, and he proposes taking up his domicile in that state. First of all, he would pay less income tax; secondly, there is no inheritance tax in the state of Florida; the President of ithe United States has in his public utterances stated that the federal authority should discontinue the collection of inheritance taxes and should leave that matter to the states alone. Does anybody in Canada believe that that will not have a marked effect upon the efflux of capital from Canada to the United States?
Just let me pause to consider what the effect will be. If the disparity is great enough the result is almost sure to be to the disadvantage of this country. Therefore I say the government should begin, and begin at once, to give some consideration to this question of income tax disparity, and to put our taxation on a level, or nearly so, with that of the neighbouring republic.
Furthermore, there has been no reduction in this country in other vexatious imposts placed upon the backs of the taxpayers by the present government. It is true that after

Neither has there been any reduction in the other direct taxation imposts made by this government since it came into power.

When we adjourned for
dinner, Mr. Speaker, I was endeavouring to enlighten some of my hon. friends to my left as to what was meant by the expression "pork barrel." I hope I made myself clear to them, and that it will not be necessary for me to advert to it at any greater length, except to reaffirm what I said in closing, that in my humble opinion any government which resorts to such political tactics in the present condition of the national finances deserves the severest disapprobation of the electorate. I do not care what political party may endeavour to take advantage of that practice, it is not the right and proper thing to do at any time, and particularly to-day when the country is in such a critical financial condition.
Now, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) in the course of his remarks on the budget made a statement, which I do not think ought to go unchallenged, with respect to the income tax collections being an index of prosperity. Even though the hon. gentleman were right in his premises, I do not think he was at all justified in the conclusions which he reached. His words were:
It may be that the wealth of the country is getting into fewer hands, that there is more wealth and also more poverty in Canada-that may be the explanation of the increased revenue from income tax. If that is true the fact is to be deplored; we do not want that condition in Canada. . . . However, I should like at some time to get an explanation from the Acting Minister of Finance as to what he thinks is the reason that more income tax is being paid in Canada under present conditions than was paid in previous years.
The official figures do not bear out in any degree the premises laid down by the hon. member; they show that there has not been an increase in the income tax collections during the last three fiscal years. I have before me a short table showing just what they were. In the fiscal year 1922-23 there was received from income tax collections 859,711,538, and from business profits taxes-the levy for which, as everybody knows, ceased after the accounting period ending December 31, 1920-there was received $13,031,461; for the fiscal year 1923-24 there was received from income tax collections $54,204,027, and on business profits taxes account, $4,752,680; while for the fiscal year 1924-25 there was received from income tax collections $56,550,000 and business profits taxes account, $2,400,000. In other words, three years ago there was collected from these two sources-and it must be borne in mind that it is all derived from income-the sum of $72,743,000, two years ago $58,956,000, 142i
and last year, $58,950,000. This all goes to show not only that the hon. gentleman was wrong in his premises, but that he was also wrong in his conclusions; and I desire to reaffirm what I said before dinner, that if the income tax rate is kept at its present standard there will be a diminution of the revenue received from this source, because those who live on income from money invested in securities will be inclined to go where the income taxation is lighter, especially when it is so easy to cross the line and avoid the heavier burden here, which has been done to my own personal knowledge in a number of cases.
In the last two budgets, Mr. Speaker, we have heard a great deal about Canada having balanced her budget. Canada has not yet balanced her budget, notwithstanding the loud professions made by the Acting Minister of Finance and those who sit around him. Last year loud professions were made that this had been done to the extent of a surplus of $35,000,000. Now, surpluses are made up in various ways. Anyone who has a knowledge of accounting, or who has anything to do with large business organizations, knows that surpluses are very largely matters of bookkeeping; and it is because of the method of bookkeeping adopted by the government that they were able to show what I consider was a fictitious surplus of $35,000,000 last year, and of $1,800,000 this year. It will not do to say to the country that "we simply followed the practice of our predecessors in office," The present government may or may not have done that; I do not know. We are led to believe they have done it, by reason of the certificate which has been given to the government balance sheet by the chartered accountants employed by the government for that purpose; that is to say, that the balance sheet was made up in the same manner as it had been made up in previous years. I presume that is a correct statement of what the gentlemen found. But that does not tell the story that the country desires to know at this time. It is desirable, other things being equal, that the budget should be balanced; I think we ought all to strive after that. But the government ought not, in honesty to themselves and in honesty to the country, to say they have balanced the budget as long as they have to pay out such enormous sums every year to the Canadian National Railways,-in cash, very largely, when they have it; otherwise, by way of guaranteed loans. We had some very illuminating figures a few nights ago with respect to the cost of operation of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. It was shown that 71 per cent of the entire amount voted by this parliament is used up in the administrative expenses of that department, and the balance ultimately reaches the soldier, the one who is intended to be benefited. That is a state
of affairs that is little less than scandalous. It is a state of affairs which will not appeal to the soldier vote of this country.
I would also abolish the portfolio, or semiportfolio, of Solicitor General. Can anybody tell me any useful purpose that the Solicitor General of this country performs? If so, I would like to hear it. It is not obvious to the ordinary member of parliament or to the general taxpayer of this country.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: It is not a new position.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: No, it is not a new position, and I am not blaming any particular government for it. It has been used as a matter of patronage among all governments, so far a3 I understand, since its establishment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
If my memory
serves me right, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) has occupied that position.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
And I have no doubt he
did it well, as he does everything else well. While he was there I have no doubt that he was a very useful official because he is that type of man who could never lie idle and draw his salary without earning it.
Then I would, and perhaps first of all, abolish the portfolio of Secretary of State, not because that portfolio is held by the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) at all, for he and I are personally the very best of friends, but I believe that the position is neither useful nor ornamental. I think the government could very well be cut down to the extent of these four portfolios.
But I would not stop there. I think the number of members in this House should be cut down. The time will come when, if this country grows as it ought to grow, and if we preserve the same ratio as laid down in the British North America Act, we shall have 500 members in this House. We have always been over-governed in Canada, and the cost of government federal, provincial and municipal, is per capita away beyond what it is in any other Anglo-Saxon country that I know of and away beyond the means of this country. I know it is easy enough to say that. Members have to run elections, and they have to go to great expense to run elections. It costs a considerable amount of money to live in Ottawa. A paternal government takes in income tax about 10 per cent of the $4,000 indemnity members receive, and after the four or five months' time the members put in in this House they will have a residuum if they live as they ought to live in Ottawa, of about $1,600. Nevertheless, I for one am willing to
The Budget-Mr. Hanson

slice off $1,000 of the indemnity if we could have any guarantee that the length of the sessions would be cut down.

speechtext:
And you would never
come back.

gentleman to vote for cutting down the indemnity, because he has no other visible means of support, so far as I know.
Then in addition, under the present conditions that obtain in this country, there should be a stop once for all to the practice of the guaranteeing of bonds for purposes Which are not strictly of federal concern. I do not intend to go into details in regard to this, but I would just like to say this, at the risk of being misunderstood, misinterpreted and misquoted:	I do not see what federal
responsibility this country had for the guaranteeing of bonds for a new bridge across the St. Lawrence at Montreal.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Go the limit.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: It is an accomplished fact now, and it not much use to talk about it, for the country is committed to the expenditure. I do not for one moment say that that bridge is not necessary: I do not know enough about the local situation to know whether it is or not, but I did try in vain for twenty minutes last year to extract from the Minister of Railways some logical reason why this expenditure should be one of federal concern, and I failed to get it. Now it is not because it is Montreal that lam saying this. I would make the same remark if it was about Tory Toronto; I will make the same remark about the erection of grain elevators at Prince Rupert and Halifax.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

I do not see any reason
myself why they should not do it all, and that suggestion was made last year by the leader of the opposition.

My memory does not serve me as to what was in the bill, but I never could see why that was a matter of federal responsibility. I do not wish to be understood as saying that the work was not an important work or a work that was not required, though I have some doubts about it.
I think it will be a detriment to property of the government already existing, but it may be that with the increase of traffic,

especially tourist traffic, as has been stated on the floor of this House, that a new bridge is necessary; but if so, I do submit that that is in no sense a federal responsibility, and that is the point I am making.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Is the hon. member opposed to the federal government giving any aid towards the construction of that bridge?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
For the benefit of the
hon. gentleman I will say this: We are committed to the principle now, and it is not much use to kick against the pricks.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
That does not
answer my question.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
That is the answer I give
to the hon. gentleman. I know the hon. gentleman wants to go down to Montreal next week or at the next election and say that the Tory party was against the bridge across the St. Lawrence. That is exactly what he desires, but he is not going to get me into that trap.
Some twenty-five years ago I went to school in the city of Halifax and they had a grain elevator there then, but I never heard of a tramp steamer or even a liner taking a cargo of grain out of that elevator, although it may be so. At the same time the people of Halifax have an aspiration for that port to be a grain shipping port. It may achieve that aspiration and if it does that elevator will be of some use. But I must say, and I speak for myself alone, that I have very grave doubts about it just as I have in the case of Prince Rupert. But a grain elevator at Vancouver, or at Montreal, or at St. John is a very different proposition. We all know that grain is one of the most liquid of commodities, and a difference of one-sixteenth of a cent a bushel in the carrying charges will lead grain to the nearest ocean port. That is the difficulty we are faced with in the Maritime provinces in our endeavour to build up national winter ports, but this is a difficulty which I feel sure will be overcome if we are able to enlist the sympathy and support not only of the railway, the common carriers of the country, but of the grain shippers as well.
There is another matter I should like to advert to in connection with this question of a balanced budget and a reduction of expenditure, and it is this: I should like to know how many motor vehicles there are in this city belonging to the government, that are used by heads of departments and (other officers of the public service? It seems to

The Budget-Mr. Hanson
me that you cannot cross one of the public streets of this city without stumbling in front of a car that is owned by the Canadian government. This thing may have been justified in war-time-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Are you afraid of them?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I try to get out of their way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: You can side-step pretty good.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: I want to say that the people of the country are beginning to learn about this extravagant practice of members of the government, heads of departments, and chief officers of the public service having cars bought and placed at their disposal. No commercial house in Canada would think of going to the extent that the government has gone in this matter. I know how easy it is for a practice like this to grow up. One cabinet minister has as much right to a private motor car as another; one deputy minister has as much right to a private motor car as another. You have only to go into the civic arena to understand how this practice grows overnight. Anybody who has had any municipal experience knows that permanent heads of departments, the moment they get into office, will begin to slip on to the corporation the cost of services that should be borne out of their private income. Why, only last week in the city council in this city the statement was made that Ottawa was paying 16,000 a year to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada for private telephones for civic employees. Some of these no doubt are justified but I venture to say, without having any personal knowledge of the circumstances, that the great majority of them are unjustified. I know that in my own city the same practice has grown up. So much for thalt. You cannot balance your budget in this country by a process of increased taxation. It must be done by a process of saving not at the bunghole but at the tap.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext: Order.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
I do not know what the hilarity is about nor do I care.
I desire now to say a word or two briefly with respect to the creation of the tariff board. I d>o not understand that any result of magnitude will come from the creation of this board. At the same time if it is to be used in an advisory capacity, if the board is not to become a bureaucracy and take the place of the elected representative of the people
upon whom the responsibility properly devolves I have not great opposition to it. It is true that in 1912 the government of Sir Robert Borden proposed to establish just such a board as, I understand, is now proposed by the Acting Minister of Finance. It is also true that the Acting Minister of Finance, and those who surround him and now have seats in this chamber, voted against the creation of that board and against the principle involved. That is perfectly characteristic of the Liberal party as all history shows. But from the standpoint of the present government the creation of this tariff board will serve two purposes which are highly desirable from the government's point of view. First, it will delegate responsibility to other than the elected representatives of the people, and it will be an excuse for continued refusal on the part of the government to face squarely the most momentous issue of the day-what is to be the fiscal policy of this country. In other words it will give the government further opportunity to say to the electors "We have created a tariff board which will advise us as to what we should do with respect to the fiscal policy." On the other hand it will be a delegation of authority and a lapse from the principle of responsible government, which procedure the government has invariably followed since it came into power. To go back to the period of 1922 when the freight rates question became acute in Canada. Had we had responsible government, as understood under British institutions, in this country the government of the day would have had a policy on the question. But what did it do.' It delegated to a committee of this House the powers that the government itself should have assumed, and it is doing the same thing with respect to the ocean-lake freight rates question. This brings me to a very brief consideration

speechtext: What is the ocean-lake freights question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: The ocean freight rates question? You will hear something more about it a little later on.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
The government took u,p the lake freight rates question and what was the result? It had to take into its own arms again and suppress its own baby. The history of the last two years will tell us that. The same thing has happened to the Petersen contract: It has been put into the discard, and the gov-
The Budget-Mr. Hanson

ernment's responsibilities have been delegated to a committee presided over by the genial member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) to devise ways and means for a policy that the government itself should devise.
This brings me-and I shall be very brief- to a consideration of what should' be the future fiscal policy of this country; and I want to lay it down as axiomatic having regard to our geographical position-lying as we do to the north for three thousand miles of the most highly protected country in the world; having regard to the fact that all Anglo-Saxon nations in the world-save and except the Mother Country itself if she can- be .called an exception-have adopted and are maintaining in its integrity the fiscal policy of protection- not that possibly it is the best fiscal policy in the world, not because some of us regard free trade, in the classic language of the hon member for Chambly-Vercheres as a pious dream- we are forced by necessity, we are forced by the very force of circumstances themselves to adopt a protective policy. What are those circumstances in 'brief? Over there across the line you have the most highly industrialized nation on earth; over there across the line you have labour organized in its highest form ; over there as a result you have the highest wages, the highest current wages, paid. I grant that under a system of protection you have high wages.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Oh, no.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Well, I never heard of low wages in a protected country unless the currency of that country had depreciated or the land had been devastated by war. At all events in the United States the results have been as I have described. The United States maintains a system of high protection, a system of standard unionized wages, and Canada by sheer force of necessity, by sheer force of	circumstances, is
obliged to meet her with the same weapon. It will not do, to pull down your tariff walls so long as you are confronted with that condition. What would happen? Let me illustrate. Down in the Maritime provinces and in that portion of the province of Quebec which lies contiguous to the American border we are side by side with the states of Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont. For the most part these states are not manufacturing and are not industrial. They are engaged in agriculture, lumbering and the like. New England is highly industrialized. The states of Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont have been the hinterland always, since I can remember and for years before, for the industrial

centres of New England. If you pull down the tariff wall and allow the free entry of American goods into Canada and allow our raw material to go out, the Maritime provinces and that part of Quebec which lies contiguous to the American states will simply become the hinterland of industrial New England. We have had gestures made and the people of this country are uncertain as to the future. The boot and shoe manufacturers are very uncertain. The textile manufacturers, especially those in the cotton industry, are very uncertain of the future. Permit me to say that the boot and shoe industry of this country is no combine. There is the keenest kind of competition in the boot and shoe manufacturing industry, and very largely and from the very beginning it has been a case of the survival of the fittest. But if the duty is taken off boots and shoes, as may reasonably be contemplated if the government give way to the arguments of some hon. gentlemen on my left, and if the duty is taken off cotton and cotton textiles, what will happen to the four cotton mills now running in the province of New Brunswick? I will tell you. Just so long as they can stagger under the swamping of the local market by the American manufacturers, they will stagger. When they are wiped out the American manufacturer will have the market to himself, up will go the-prices, we will pay the piper, and we will have to pay higher prices for textiles than previously.

speechtext:

know if the hon. gentleman is aware that during the year 1818 or 1919 some of the textile companies in this country made as high as 330 per cent, on the capital invested? That fact was brought out before the High Cost of Living committee.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: The hon. member is referring to war times. I am speaking of normal times. You will never see a condition like that again.

I know that in the New England states they manufacture a million yards of textiles to every yard we manufacture in Canada. Their overhead is so much less, and their raw material so much nearer that we can not successfully compete. My hon. friends to my left and1 all free traders in the House will say " Then you should not be allowed to compete". I am not in favour of that line of reasoning. I believe that we should endeavour to build up an industrial.

life in this country, even though it may not be, to use a well-worn phrase in this House, indigenous to the country itself. I see no reason why boots and shoes for Canadians should not be made in my city and in the cities of Montreal and Quebec. I see no reason why we should not manufacture the cotton textiles that we use in this country, and give employment to Canadian workmen who will be able to maintain happy homes. But let the reverse take place and what will happen? You will immediately see the emigration of our skilled mechanics across the line. They will not go back to the farms, even if they came from them, and we will be hewers of wood and drawers of water.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Will not my hon. friend admit that at present the cotton industry is bad in the United States, bad in England and bad all over the world?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
My hon. friend may be an authority on the cotton industry. I am not. All I know is that in my community the cotton industry is working from hand to mouth, and the men have been employed three and four days a week since this government came into power. I think the tariff on cotton should be raised a little so as to keep out the surplus of cotton goods manufactured outside of the country, and have the goods manufactured at home. You cannot build up a diversified nation if you are all going to be miners, farmers or fishermen. You will never have a home market that is worth a bawbee for the farmers if you do not have some industrial life in the country, and, as far as industries that are native to the country are concerned, I say that unless we take some steps to preserve our own raw material we wall not have it very much longer. If the newsprint mills, the pulp mills and paper mills continue to grow as they have grown in this country, and if the ravages of the forests by insect pests and fire continue as in the past, then that great industry in Canada will indeed be a short-lived one, and we had better look out for the future. This country does not need a high tariff. I im not in favour of a tariff which would absolutely keep out all sorts of imports, but I am in favour of such an adequate tariff as would allow our manufacturers to compete in our home market. That is what we want; if we are able to do a little more and take in some export trade, so much the better, and I think we should attempt to do it However, it is not possible in certain lines.
As far as my constituency is concerned, if has never yet-and it is half agricultural- voted in favour of low tariff, and I do no' think it is going to begin now.

I leave it to the judgment of hon. members to my left. objection to the hon. member for Hants asking a question, but I should like him to put one question at a time, not half a dozen at once. With respect to the duty on coal, I had not the Nova Scotia situation in my mind when I was speaking of it; I was making a constructive suggestion in the interests of the coal producers of the Maritime provinces.
At first blush it seemed to me that the minister's proposed export tax on power was a new avenue for revenue that the country might very well adopt, and I was rather favourably disposed towards it. If we were sending power out of the country for the first time, if power companies in New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario were not tied up by long term contracts; in other words, if it could be assured that the levy would be passed along to the consumer in the United States, by whom it should properly be borne, then I say it would be a very good source of revenue. If it could be considered from that standpoint alone, then I would tell the minister that his tax is not high enough, and that he could very easily make it considerably higher. Perhaps I ought not to speak dogmatically about this, not having full information before me. But let me tell the minister that nearly all of these hydro electric developments which have been initiated by private capital had to tie up to long term cheap contracts with consumers in the United States along the border. I have in mind the New Brunswick Power Company, which develops hydro electric power just within the borde' between New Brunswick and Maine. This company was organized and its bonds were sold to the public both in New Brunswick
The Budget-Mr. Hanson

and in Maine. Before it could get a dollar from the investing public it had to show
that it had made contracts lasting the lifetime of the bonds and producing sufficient revenue not only to pay carrying charges but also operating expenses. Is it quite fair to companies so situated-and I have no interest in this particular company-to have their export power taxed?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, probably it is a fortunate circumstance that the Progressive party have their turn to speak once in a while. I desire, Sir, at the outset to compliment the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the very compact, concise and lucid manner in which he presented this budget-not that I agree with him in all respects, but this is simply a friendly word of commendation. It is most regrettable that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has been unable to be with us during the present session. The people of Canada owe him a deep debt of gratitude for his unswerving loyalty to the country and of appreciation for the ability which has characterized his service.
Before entering upon a discussion of the budget itself I wish to try to show to the House that although it has been said on many occasions that the United States is the most highly protected country in the world, if we examine the facts we will find that it is not such a highly protected country after all. Such assertions, Mr. Speaker, as this-that the United States is the most highly protected country-entirely disregard the facts and anyone who makes them must be unwilling to limit himself to what he .believes to be the truth. If those who put forth these claims ever looked to the facts they would be ashamed to advance such fallacious contentions. The United States collected, in round
figures, $566,136,864 during the year 1923 through customs taxes, as against 118 millions in Canada for the same year. It is obvious that the division of this total amongst the population of 110 millions to the south of us produces an average of $5.04 per capita, whilst the Canadian average on a population of 9 millions is about $14.55 per head, a difference of $9.51 per head against Canada. At the Canadian rate the customs revenue of the United States would amount to $1,457,000,000, while the Canadians customs revenue on the American rate would only be $32,000,000. Our customs tariff imposes a burden four times greater than the American tariff, yet it is claimed that our neighbours are more highly protected.
For my part I would be satisfied for the time being if the government consented to remove that part of the customs burden which is in excess of that of the United States. That would still leave us, as my hon. friends to the right are prone to claim we should be, a highly protected country.

I do not think it
would. I have the highest appreciation of my right hon. friend's clear intellect and keen debating power; at the same time, I do not see how he can get away from my argument. What does this additional burden mean to the head of a family of five? In the United States he pays $20.20 to the customs gate; in Canada he pays $77.75, a difference of about $50. Low tariff is the essential requirement for the progress of our nation. No purely protective tariff or preference can result in anything but the imposition of unnecessary burdens on the people. Tariffs are a hindrance to natural trade, a hindrance to natural development. They achieve everything, Sir, except the results they are intended to produce. How are we to estimate the burden carried by a nation if we do not estimate the amount of the burden carried by each individual? If the amount carried by each individual is greater in Canada than it is in

The Budget-Mr. King (Huron)
the United States, where will the young men of Canada be apt to go? To the United States, of course-we understand that perfectly well. I was talking only last evening to a man in this city who is in the bond business. He said:	"I find I can do far better in the
United States than I can in Canada. If I stay in Canada, my sons and my grandsons and my great grandsons will be loaded down with heavy taxation; the burden will never go off their shoulders. But in the United States such is not the case." Can we not remedj' the conditions in Canada? I say to this government and to all future governments: Try to reduce the load of taxation; try to economize in every possible way and before many years we may be put on an even basis with the United States.
I claim that regardless of the fallacious contentions that have been made, a low tariff policy would not throw us politically into the arms of the United States. Notwithstanding the attempted arguments to show that protection was and is the safeguard of our national independence, I say, Sir, that if any policy will tend to loosen the bonds of our national unity it is the policy of protection such as we have at present-a policy that creates discontent, a policy that prevents the Canadian citizen from enjoying the decent living conditions to which he is entitled. Who can deny, however, that on the other hand a policy of low tariff which will result in contentment, which will permit sane and rapid developments, a policy which will enable progress along the channels given to us by our natural conditions, will in itself bring about a more strongly welded union; will form a democracy that no storm can shatter; will build up a country which we will be proud to live in and make us zealous of our institutions and our independence.
What Canada needs to-day is reciprocity with the United States. As I have just said, political unrest results from economic discontent, and if this were removed the talk of secession and annexation would then fall on deaf ears. The sentiments which hold Canada to the British Empire would be proof against every attack if our economic conditions were rectified.
I propose to try to show in my humble way that if this government and future governments will do their best not to enter into a commercial or tariff war with the United States, we are on the eve of better trade relations with that country. We have the word of President Coolidge himself that the United States is just on the eve of being a great importing nation of agricultural products. We

also have the word of a great many financial experts in the United States.
On account of the large credits, loans and investments made abroad by the United States, it becomes certain that the nations to whom these loans were made will have to pay for them by exports to the United States. One plan calls for a progressive "liberalization" of the tariff policy of the United States not necessarily immediately, but very soon as a necessary adjustment to permit that country to make the larger importations of foreign goods required by her new position as a creditor nation.
I am going to quote the views of certain financial gentlemen in the United States. First is a statement by Francis H. Sisson, vicepresident of the Guaranty Trust Company, to the effect that the tariff had been a "foreign element" in the natural working of economic laws, and part of the normal adjustment would be a lowering of it.
George E. Roberts, vice-president of the National City Bank, and formerly United States Comptroller of the Currency, speaking on this point, said:
A difficulty as regards the receipt of interest payments may in the future arise unless our high tariff is changed. I do not think that this will make any great difference in the next two or three years or so, but the tariff is essentially an anomaly in our foreign trade, and our business men will have to adjust themselves to the necessity of competing more with foreign products and get into lines in which they can do so most advantageously. But these changes, I believe, will come about naturally through the pressure of circumstances.
Prof. Eugene E. Agger, of Columbia University, said:
A liberalization of the tariff is certain to come about as a result ot the increase of foreign investments The change might come through the rise of foreign tariffs until they more or less neutralize ours, but I think it is more likely to come through a change of feeling here.
The situation is, of course, that the consumers of goods are not organized and so cannot readily make themselves felt when the tariff provisions are being made; but I think that the producers themselves, who can make themselves felt readily, will more and more seek to lower the rate on manufactured goods so that foreign countries can pay for them by selling their products here.
The farmers and the cotton producers and some other interests are already beginning to seek a reduction in the tariff, because they are discovering that their most logical line of attack, to return to their former relation to the manufacturers, is not to support a measure like the McNary-Haugen bill to raise their prices, but rather to bring down the prices of manufactured goods.
The tariff, of course, has got into general talk to such an extent that it is being credited for more than it is worth. There are so many other factors in manufacturing that, in many cases, there is not much more justification for a high tariff on goods coming into this country than there is for a similar tariff between various parts of the country. And the change in our position from debtor nation to creditor, will help to

The Budget-Mr. King (Huron)
make this fact appreciated, and will bring a demand for more moderate rates.
Dr. Benjamin M. Anderson, Jr., of the Chase National Bank, provided some of the Chase economic bulletins, in which he has expressed his views. In one of these he pointed out the changed economic conditions which make a moderate tariff policy vitally important to-day, and explained that:
Exports must be paid for by imports, and that a country which wishes to sell abroad must also be willing to buy in foreign countries if foreign trade is not to result in credit congestion and reaction.
The change will make for a permanently balanced industrial situation, far more satisfactory and far more dependable than the temporary unstable equilibria on which we have built temporary periods of activity since the Armistice. We need not fear Europe's revival or seek to defer it by placing tariff walls in the way.
The position of the farmer has been injured rather than helped by the general tariff policy. It has not enabled him, for the most part, to get more for what he had to sell. On the contrary, by lessening Europe's purchasing power in the American markets, it has lessened the ability of his foreign customer to buy. and thus made his prices lower than they would have been.
The whole trouble to-day, Mr. Speaker, is the lack of purchasing power in the agricultural districts of this country, and no one knows that better than the Massey-Harris Company of Toronto, and Mr. Bradshaw; no one knows it better than the heads of the manufacturing concerns. I know conditions among the farmers. I know that the fanners are economizing in every way possible. I know they are making binders, ploughs and mowers that should have been in t'he fence comer long ago, do the work to-day. They are using all their implements in that fashion, fixing them up, because they have not the purchasing power; they simply cannot buy. I am not a pessimist, and the farmers of the county of Huron whom I have the honour to represent are not pessimists. They are not decrying Canada, but the}' are looking for better times to come, and they are looking for these better times to come by a reduction of the tariff along certain lines. I wish to point out to the Acting Minister of Finance that they are looking for a reduction of the tariff on automobiles, textiles, woollens, boots and shoes. They are not looking for reductions on very many lines; I myself do not believe in a complete upturn of the tariff almost every year. We should have a revision of the tariff at certain periods, every five or six or seven or ten years, as the case may be. for our manufacturers must have a chance. They must know that the tariff is not going to be interfered with for a certain number of years.
I think probably that state of affairs can be brought about, but at the present time the tariff is not down to where it ought to be.
Just recently an Alberta farmer sent to the Citizen a copy of a statement of a sale of stock, showing that he had received $54.44 for seven head of cattle-which is less than $8 per head. The stock ranged in weight from 580 pounds to 1,240 pounds, and they were high grade cattle, not scrub stuff. On the back of the statement the farmer wrote, "Why settlers leave the farm after being on same for twenty years."
The prosperity of Canadian industry is very largely dependent upon the purchasing power of the farmers. They must either earn sufficient money to buy goods at the present level of Canadian prices, or the level of prices must be reduced to come within the range of the farmer's income under deflation.
The tariff is maintained to prevent the farmer buying at reduced prices, but the tariff is no protection against the reduction of wheat and cattle prices.	It as doubtful
whether tariff reductions would restore the purchasing power of the Canadian farmers without depriving an equal number of workers in the protected industries of purchasing power. I wish to read, with the permission of the House a short article from the Listening Post:
So the farmers of Canada, and the townspeople who are dependent on them for their livelihood, see the prices of the varied goods which modern industrial economy compels them to buy enhanced by tariff duties. They see indications that the profits of those who own the factories are also enhanced. They see the products of these factories sold abroad, when competition compels, at lower prices than they themselves can buy them. And they smart under a sense of injustice. Forced to accept for their own products prices fixed by competition in the open markets of the world, they are compelled to buy for their own needs at prices increased by deliberate legislative action. Naturally and inevitably they are driven to ask why this injustice should continue? To ask how long they can hope to compete in the free world markets if their costs of living and production are artificially raised? To sell in the cheapest market and to buy in the dearest is an inversion of that condition which is clearly the selfinterest of everyone to enjoy. Who can expect that the Western farmers should meekly and uncomplainingly accept such a sacrifice of their obvious interest?
Now, Sir, in connection with what I said with respect to the United States I wish to put on Hansard the following schedule showing the prices of cattle at Toronto, Winnipeg and Chicago:
