Is it any wonder that the farmers of Canada are casting longing eyes on the markets in the country to the south? They see perfectly well that the market there is really their natural miarket. If the Canadian government would see to it that no tariff war takes place between the two Countries, and if the relations between Canada and the United States are conducted in a spirit of brotherly kindness, the day is not far distant when we shall have access to that market.
Now, Sir, I want to make a brief reference to Great Britain. What country in the world has made such a rapid recovery from the ravages of -the Great war as Great Britain has done?	Free trade has proven the
economic salvation of that wonderful land. This, Mr. Speaker, is so well recognized that all parties in England to-day unite in supporting a motion before the British parliament providing for the repeal of the Safeguarding of Industries Act.
Honourable members to my right are prone to accuse those who sit in this section of the House of representing a class. But, Mr. Speaker, even should this assertion be true is it not still a greater truth in so far as these hon. gentlemen themselves are concerned? We at least can say that the workers in our cities will benefit as well as the farmers from a low tariff policy. In their case it is the height of folly to attempt to maintain that even the manufacturers, whose friends they claim to be, will derive any benefits of a permanent nature from the high protection they advocate. I ask honourable members whether the child of the poor family raised under "catch-as-catch-can" conditions, or the petted and protected spoiled only child of the rich man, can best sail the troubled seas of our everyday world. We may represent a class, Mr. Speaker, but if we do, it is the far larger class, the class that needs representation most urgently and the class which, up to the present, has had the least of it. These utterances from hon. gentlemen to my right have no foundation in fact. They only misrepresent the conditions which they endeavour to portray. The sooner the manufacturer and his representative come down to the earth of the farmer and of the working man, the sooner will we, in this parliament, be able to bring about conditions satisfactory to all and detrimental to none. Yes, Sir, the manufacturer has a right to representation, but who will deny the same right to the farmer and to the worker? Why must .the farmer grow the bread required for the sustenance of the manufacturer? Why must the labourer sweat and

slave to provide him with dividends? Why again should our natural development be hindered so as to nurture the manufacturers' growth? No, Mr. Speaker, we can never expect better conditions to prevail, so long as we maintain conditions that do not evenly distribute the load of our national obligations.
It has often been stated in this House, and more frequently by honourable members to my right, that the prices of farm produce are regulated by world conditions over which no individual country has control. Let us apply the same principle to our manufacturers, and allow the prices for the articles which they produce to be guided by the world supply and demand of the commodities they offer for sale. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that a condition which is fair for one section of our population is also fair for the other sections. One must be intentionally blind to all conditions of fairness and have swallowed his principles of British fair play to advocate in this democratic Dominion one set of standards for our manufacturers and another for our farmers and working classes.
I admit that the United States are living at present under a protective system, but I have no hesitation in predicting that this condition will not long endure in that country. You may be sure, Mr. Speaker, that the farmers in the country to the south will not much longer endure a policy which has been so detrimental to their welfare. Yes, I repeat, the tariff has done for the American farmer just the reverse of what he expected from it. He asked to be protected against Canadian wheat and he obtained, some time ago a protection of thirty cents a bushel. At that time the price of wheat on the Chicago market was six cents per bushel higher than the price prevailing at Winnipeg. He was not satisfied with that- and obtained, more recently, from the United States government an additional protection of 12 cents, bringing the total to 42 cents a bushel. What has been the result? What did the United States farmer gain by this protection? Well, this is it. With no protection the Chicago price was at an advance of six cents over the Winnipeg one. With a protection of 42 cents a bushel against Canadian wheat, the advantage in price at Chicago has dropped to-day to two cents below Winnipeg. What a wonderful protective achievement.
I have admitted, Mr. Speaker that the United States is at present living under a protective tariff, but I take the most emphatic stand against the claims advanced that it is the most highly protected country in the world. When we take into consideration that

The Budget-Mr. King (Huron)
almost 58 per cent of the total imports of the United States are admitted free of duty; and we find that in the year 1924 the average rate of duty on dutiable imports into Canada was 22.85 per cent, and into the United States 35.51 per cent, and' also in the same year in regard to the average rate of duty on total imports, the rate in Canada was 15.13 per cent and in the United States 15.33 per cent, we at once come to the conclusion that the United States has a small amount of goods under higher protective duty than Canada.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, low tariff is the essential requirement for the progress of our nation. No purely protective tariff or preference can result in anything but the imposition of unnecessary burdens upon the people. Tariffs are a hindrance to natural trade. They are a hindrance to natural development and they achieve everything except the results which they are intended to produce. *
Who wants Imperial preference? Surely not the people of the British Isles. Why should they desire any measure which will increase their cost of living? Do we want Imperial preference? Not unless our British sentiments are limited by the benefits that would accrue to us from a partial Closing of the Old Land markets to other nations, to the detriment of Britishers; not unless our attachment to British institutions is so weak as to wish our lot to be made better by the imposition of burdens on our brothers.
Previous to the Imperial conference two years ago, a meeting of members of all parties in England, was held in the House of Commons to formulate a policy of defence against the demands which it appeared certain would be made for Imperial preference. I quote a few of the remarks made by Mr. Asquith on that occasion. He said:
From the beginning of the controversy begun twenty years ago the issue raised by the call for Imperial preference was the taxation of food. Mr. Joseph Chamberlain at the very outset confessed that any preference given to the colonies or the outlying parts of the empire was of no use, economically or sentimentally, unless as an essential part of it you put a tax on the importation of food into this country.
There has been no change in the essential, fundamental and unalterable economic conditions. Imperial preference without taxation of food is a fraud and a sham.
If that issue is raised again-and it will be raised and must be raised by some of the proposals to be laid before the forthcoming Imperial economic conference- and if some of these proposals materialize, the issue ought to be put fairly and squarely before the public, I have not the slightest doubt if that is done the verdict will be just as it was in 1906.
And! the matter was placed before the British public, Mr. Speaker, and their verdict was just as emphatic as in 1906. Can we 143
blame them? Why should they increase their cost of living? Mr. Asquith is right in maintaining that any idea of Imperial preference must necessarily mean the taxation of food and it is just as true of any tariff measure. I, for one, am unalterably opposed to any policy that will force the people of the British Isles to remember our ingratitude at their breakfast tables.
Speaking at Vancouver the late President Warren G. Harding said:
The best citizen is the man who is a good neighbour and the best neighbour is the man whom we are friendly enough with to go and borrow a coupls of eggs from.
This, Sir, may sound to you as an obvious truth. The regrettable part is that though we feel those sentiments of neighbourly friendliness we appear at the same time to be very unwilling to adopt the practice of the true brotherhood which they teach. What can be thought of brothers who hamper their own relations by the detrimental tariff walls which exist between the two great nations of this North American continent. I say to the people of Canada and to those of the United States that friendly relations and the feeling of brotherhood will only grow in proportion to the ease with which they can carry on both their commercial and diplomatic relations. The brotherhood of our two countries will indeed only be one of true Christianity when we can deal amongst ourselves between our respective countries as we or they are dealing to-day between our own cities.
The tariff must be looked at as absolutely vicious and the more you look at all its intricacies the more you realize that it never did and never can accomplish the purpose for which it was adopted. Tariffs the world over, in no matter what form they occur, have always been unfair as between different industries. They have always caused trouble and friction between nations. They always engender commercial rivalry and sooner or later they have ended in strained relations between nations, in many cases culminating in disastrous struggles in diplomacy, eventually ending in open war and the consequent destruction of humanity. What can any one advance in support of a policy that leads to such an end?
I was especially pleased, Mr. Speaker, that this government cut their moorings during the session of 1924 and' made a distinct cleavage between tfhe proponents of low tariff and the advocates of high protection. At



The Budget-Mr. King (Huron)
the same time, Mr. Speaker, I am very much disappointed that they did not in the least degree continue the lead then given. If confirmation is required, I need only read the statement made by the Prime Minister himself whilst addressing some remarks to the hon. member for St. Lawrence and St. George (Mr. Marler). In the course of that debate the Prime Minister said:
The die is now cast. From this time forward, Mr. Speaker, we have the two natural alignments in this House, high and low tariff advocates.
Now, I am disappointed that the government did not at least lower the duties on such articles as automobiles, rubber and a few other things.
The manufacturers of our urban centres had better realize immediately that the population of our rural communities have finally set out with a determination to make a finish fight, a winning one, you may be sure, in order to equalize the conditions which have so long been discriminatory to our farming people. Previous to this parliament, the interests, the requirements and the needs of the rural centres received at best but scant consideration. Perhaps it was their fault. Very few men in previous parliaments had the full knowledge of farm conditions, due to the fact that in a great number of cases the representatives were the products of urban centres. This lack of representation as compared with the over representation of the manufacturing interests, resulted in the conditions which are to be found to-day when the farmer finds himself at such a disadvantage that it is just possible, by real hard1 work, to eke out a meagre living. On the other hand the agriculturists of this country do not wish to create unrest and dissatisfaction in any section of our population. They are the most stable part of our people. They certainly do not desire radicalism in any form. They are out to teach our manufacturers that they can progress better on their own supports and that the high tariff protection they have been accustomed to has not and never will give them strength. The farming population are not looking for favours. They are as willing as ever to bear their just share of our national burden. They are only asking that the hole be bored in the centre of the evener so that each section will have an even draught. They have now rebelled and certainly will not continue the slavery imposed upon them by drilling, always further from the centre, the hole that determines the respective pull required of the members of our national team.
No; Mr. Speaker, a high tariff policy is deterimental to the sound, sane and effective

development of any country. No results of a permanent nature can obtain under such artificial conditions. We had better be without industries, if to possess them we must compel their growth within the protective walls of a hothouse. I am convinced that the diagnosis of our manufacturing industries was erroneous, since the treatment prescribed has proven ineffective. With the experience of the mistake made it is our bounden duty to rectify the error by changing the medicine. What better proof have we of this than the oft repeated plea of industry that it cannot stand on its own feet. The manufacturer is like the spoiled child of an over indulgent parent. I admit that this young man, might suffer by too radical a change in treatment. We must, however, gradually reduce the doses and finally omit altogether the support which he has too long received and imbue him with that spirit of confidence in himself that will enable him to depend soMy on his manhood for success.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive party is a modest, retiring party, and we have been subjected to political thrusts, some of them not very clean, from all sides of the House-even from our own side; but I desire to affirm right here, that not only will the Progressive party come back after the next election, but will come back more than a mere remnant-more than a sad remnant. The Progressive party is here to do business and will do business in this House after all the present members, I was going to say, had passed into oblivion, but I do not say that because I know there are a great many hon. members of this House whose names will go down in the annals of Canadian history. I say the Progressive party will be doing business in this House long after all the present members have passed from this earthly stage of existence. The Progressive party has its roots in the soil and they will not be very easily eradicated.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to state at the outset that it is my purpose to support the budget proposals as brought down by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and, in as brief a manner as possible, to give a few reasons for doing so. A short time ago we had a speech

The Budget-Mr. Robinson
on the budget from the leader of the Progressive group (Mr. Forke), and I remember that he stated that he deprecated the fact that the financial statement had not been given to us in such a form that the ordinary person could readily unerstand it. I quite agree with him and I too would wish that the financial statement had been made to th:s House in such a manner that the ordinary person who was not a financial expert could easily understand it. We find the government classifying as assets items which the opposition classify as liabilities. As long as our financial experts disagree, how can those of us who have not an expert financial knowledge, draw a conclusion from the financial statement as presented to us? I have gone back in history a little and I find that this is not by any means a new condition of things. If you will read the history of parliaments, you will find that every government endeavours to make the best showing it can. Every government attempts to keep alive a feeling of contentment in the minds of the people, while it seems to be the duty of the opposition, if possible, to break down that financial statement and to preach discontent. Therefore, I am not at all surprised when this debate follows the regular order. I am ready, however, to accept the statement of the Acting Minister of Finance concerning our surplus, for this reason. Last year we were face to face with the same conditions that we are facing to-day. The Acting Minister of Finance at that time claimed that we had a surplus of some $34,000,000. This was strenuously denied by the opposition, and yet during the year we are told that the government made a payment of about $34,000,000 on the national debt. They must have had this sum in order to be able to pay it, and I am therefore ready to accept the statement of the Acting Minister of Finance that we have, at this time, a surplus of $1,800,000.
The equalization, if I may call it such, of the duties on coal also meets with my approval, for this reason. I am not going into the detaHte of the history of the duties on coal. It is sufficient to say that there were two duties on slack coal, one of 14 cents and the other of 53 cents a ton. As usual, it was the manufacturer who had the advantage of the 14 cent rate while the householder paid 53 cents a ton. If there is to be a duty on coal, there should be no special privileges to any class; all classes should pay the same duty, and for that reason, I do not look on the change in the duties on coal as an increase. It is an increase to the manufacturer from 14 cents to 50 cents a ton, 143i
but to the householder it is a decrease from 53 to 50 cents a ton. I come from a county in Nova Scotia that is non-producing as regards coal. We are users of coal and I believe the householders in my county will be pleased when they know that the duty that they have to pay On coal has been reduced from 53 to 50 cents a ton.
Another item proposed by the Acting Minister of Finance that appeals to me is a tariff commission. If by this tariff commission is meant a travelling commission to go around the country and then come back and give its opinions, I for one would not see much in	it. We	have	had this kind10 p.rn.	of	thing in	days	gone by. Butif	by this	tariff	commission is
meant a number of experts who will collect facts and give us the means of forming our own opinion, I am in favour of it. I was surprised the other night when the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Hoey) said that if we had such a tariff commission, it would fasten on the country forever the system of protection. I do not believe it would, and I for one would say that if a knowledge of the facts will fasten on us the system of protection, I do not see how we can get away from it. As I take it, it will be the duty of this commission to collect facts and to submit them to .members of this House so that we can form our judgment on them, and not as the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) said a short time ago, to take the responsibility in their hands nor to assume to themselves the right to fix rates. Is this not needed? I for one would say that it is, and for this reason. Sitting in this House I have heard somebody advocate an increased rate of duty, giving reasons for his opinion, and to me it seemed to be all right, while some other hon. member would take the same industry and show that it was already too highly protected. What are the facts in such cases? Let us have -the facts and then we shall be able tq form our opinion.
I should like to mention, in passing, a budget proposal that appeals to me, and that is the reduction of the duty on engines used by fishermen. This will be a benefit to the fishermen on both the Atlantic and the Pacific.
A great deal of discussion has taken place in this House regarding trade and business depression. Everybody will admit that we have been passing through a period of serious depression. A little knowledge of history will teach us that during any war there is a .period of great business activity and this is always followed by a reaction. It cannot be cured by legislation. Any country that has engaged in
The Budget*-Mr. Robinson

a long drawn out war must ipay the penalty. The longer that country is at war the heavier the penalty it must pay. We were in the war from start to finish, and we have to face the depression that naturally follows in its wake.
I wish to speak for a minute or two on conditions in the Maritime provinces, because I am more familiar with conditions there than with those in other parts of the Dominion. We have had a serious depression, but I would point out that to a great extent this is a postwar condition. Let us take Nova Scotia, for example. During the war Halifax was a world port; all the ships of the seven seas found there a haven; the population of the city 'grew by leaps and bounds; all goods that could be sold were sold there; there was an abundant demand; for labour; and even the explosion, although so disastrous, was not altogether an evil, for it brought into the city a great many labourers to reconstruct the devastated buildings. Now with the close of the war the city goes back to normal. Could anything else be expected? It had inflated its papulation by
15,000	or 20,000. That surplus of necessity must go somewhere else, and a great deal of the exodus from Nova Scotia is accounted for by the abnormal conditions that existed in Halifax during t.h.e war. In Nova Scotia another cause of financial depression is due to the trade policy under which we have suffered more or less for the past forty years, because much as protection may ;be a benefit to other provinces-and I do not deny that it is a benefit to the central provinces-there is no question but that it has been very injurious to the Maritime provinces. We have seen all our industries either closed out or else compelled to move to the central provinces. There has been also a movement of capital. I do not say that legislation could change it, I do not say but that it is the natural result, for capital tends to flow to large industrial centres, and So far as I can see there is no way to prevent it. Four of our largest chartered banks had their origin in the Maritime provinces, but their headlquarters are not there to-day. So I say from our geographical position the trade policy that may be beneficial to the rest of Canada is injurious to us, and it has been one of the causes that has produced depression in the Maritime provinces. When hon members stand up in this House and say that such depression can be cured by some act of this parliament, I for one do not see how it can be done. Again, we used to have low transportation rates, but when the Intercolonial railway became a part of the Canadian National system our rates were substantially increased,

with the result that we are now almost isolated from the rest of Canada. The Fordney tariff struck us very hard, especially in the fishing industry, and for two or three years at least the fishing industry was disorganized. But I do not wish to paint too dark a picture. Let me speak of Nova Scotia, of what we have done there. In the statistics for 1924 I find that our field crops were valued at nearly $17,000,000; we had dairy products worth nearly $10,000,000; fruit and vegetables to the value of something over $7,000,000; poultry and eggs worth nearly $1,700,000; our fisheries yielded a revenue of $8,750,000; our minerals yielded a revenue of $24,900,000, and up to date we have shipped to England
1,900,000	barrels of apples: so the outlook for Nova Scotia is not altogether dark. But we have some needs, and it is of these I wish to speak for a few minutes.
The first and great need of the Maritime provinces, as I see it, is lower freight rates. Something should be done in order that we may be placed on an equality with the rest of the Dominion in this respect. That these freight rates are hard on the Maritime provinces has been shown conclusively by the member for Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes) and the member for Northumberland (Mr. Snowball). We are suffering from the bad effects of unjust freight rates. Now, this is the cure proposed by some people. They say that the Maritime provinces should be given a freight rate lower than actual cost, and that the rest of the Dominion should be taxed' to make up the difference. I do not believe that that is the general wish of the Maritime provinces, nor do I believe that it would produce the result that is looked for. As I understand it, we in the Maritimes do not ask for charity- not at this stage at least; all we want is justice. But there are two items in the Maritime provinces that might well receive a freight rate lower than actual cost, and this reduction would work a benefit to the entire Dominion; those two items are coal and fish. Certainly the people of Ontario and Quebec need our coal; therefore if it were broi^ht from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at a very low rate it would benefit us, and it would benefit also Ontario and Quebec. The same would be true concerning fish. But would this be true with respect to other things? Take farm products, for example. Suppose we in the Mara time provinces received a rate lower than cost in order to ship our farm products into the central provinces, see what the result would be. I have heard, hon. members of the opposition say that in Ontario at least they do not want competition.

The Budget-Mr. Robinson
in farm products; indeed they tell us that they wish farm products from the United States shut out from Ontario and Quebec, for they want to supply the home market themselves. They do not want competition. We have heard that over and over again in the House. They advocate a tariff against United States farm products. Would they be willing to have competition from the Maritime provinces in farm products? Would they be willing that we should send up our butter, out eggs, our poultry, our bacon? And not only send those commodities here, bult that a portion of the expense be paid by the central provinces to the extent to which the freight rates were lower than cost? It does not seem to me reasonable. And if we had the revival in industry that has been talked1 of down' i'n the Maritime provinces, and we began to ship manufactured goodte into the central provinces, would the manufacturers there, who already say that they do not wish for any competition, would they, I say, welcome competition from the Maritime provinces, especially if they had to bear a portion of the freight rates on the goods? It seems to me, Sir, that iit would be unreasonable to expect any such welcome.
What we need1 in the Maritime provinces is wider markets. We have developed a market in England and in some of the countries on the continent, and we have a market in the West Indies that. I believe could be developed to a very considerable degree. Of course, it goes without saying that, whether it be true for the rest of Canada ot not, reciprocity would have been a panacea for the Maritimes. However, if we had wider markets, if we had better shipping facilities, including cold storage, frost proof warehouses, improved docking, and if we had lower freight rates, it seems to me that all these things would tend to cure the present depression in -the Maritime provinces.
Now for a few minutes I wish to refer, Mr. Speaker, to something that, so far as I know, has not been dealt with except by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Hammell) who spoke a few nights ago on the tourist trade. I believe we overlook the importance of this trade. If I understand it rightly, it is the third item of revenue. From agriculture we had a revenue in 1924 of $407,000,000; from wood and1 wood products, $229,000,000; from the tourist trade, $150,000,000; from mine and mine products, $125,000,000; from animals and animal products, $135,000,000. Here is a trade question upon which, it seems to me, all parties in the House might agree. Here is an infant industry that I do not think anybody
would oppose encouraging. The encouragement of the tourist trade is an attempt to capitalize our scenery, our climate, and our points of historic interest. The tourist trade does not. interfere with any existing industries, nor does it in any way deplete our natural resources. It is well known to members of this House what other countries have done in connection with the tourist trade. Switzerland has capitalized the Alps; France has capitalized her art museums and her galleries, Italy her blue sky, and Greece her historic ruins. Therefore, it seems to me that we should try in some way to capitalize our scenery, our points of historic interest-and we have them, Mr. Speaker. I need not point out the beauties of British Columbia, the attractions of the Great Lakes or the river St. Lawrence, the historic interest that attaches to the province of Quebec. I would like, however, to say a few words about the Maritime provinces and their relation to the tourist trade, or the relation of the tourist trade to them.
In the first place, the scenery throughout the Maritime provinces all belongs in the same category. There are not in this respect, three provinces; there is one province. We have no mighty mountains; we have no great rivers. Everything is on a small scale. Geologically speaking, the Maritime provinces are the oldest parts of the continent of America; nature has been at work there the longest time, and she has smoothed out the rough places. There are no irregularities; we have harmony- harmony of river, hill and valley. We have a climate that is not equalled anywhere else in North America. The thermometer rarely goes below zero in winter or above eighty in summer; while cities of central Canada and the United States are sweltering in heat, we in the Maritime provinces are enjoying the cool breezes of the Atlantic.
But I wish to emphasize particularly our points of historic interest. We in the Maritime provinces have a number of important points of historic interest. The provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were anciently the French province of Acadie. The first settlement that was made in Canada was made at Annapolis, or Port Royal, in 1604. The French settled at various places throughout Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and whenever a war took place between England and France those points of settlement by the French were objects of attack. The result was that they were taken by the English and were handed back by treaty. Annapolis was taken four different times by the English and then returned to
The Budget-Mr. Robinson

the French. In 1713 the province of Nova Scotia was ceded to England, but almost immediately war broke out, because the French claimed that they had ceded but the peninsula of Nova Scotia while the English claimed they had been given the entire province of Acadie. The result was that the French built a fort at Beausejour, and at Louisburg, in Cape Breton, and war went on. In 1763, of course, the entire country passed into the hands of England, but between the years 1713 and 1763 there were great historic events in Nova Scotia. Fort Beausejour was taken; Louisburg was taken twice. It was in that period that Halifax was settled by the English and the expulsion of the Acadians took place. I could go on for some time pointing out the historic interest of Nova Scotia, but it is not necessary.	.
I might mention that as far as Canada is concerned we are the land of first things. The first road in Canada was built at Port Royal in 1605. The first Roman Catholic church in Canada was established in 1608. The first Protestant church in Canada was built at Halifax in 1749. The first newspaper published in Canada was published in Halifax in 1751. The first representative assembly chosen in Canada met at Halifax in 1758. The first college or institution of higher learning was founded at Windsor, Nova Scotia, in 1788. It is a fact that we shipped or had apples for sale in Nova Scotia in 1663, and coal was exported from Cape Breton in 1743. I could continue, Mr. Speaker, for some time giving a list of points of historic interest in the province of Nova Scotia.
I wish to point out briefly what we have done in connection with the tourist business. In Nova Scotia last year we had 100,000 tourists and the revenue from that source was 87,000,000. We have good roads. We have tourists' associations; we have boards of trade devoting their activities to promoting tourist trade. We distributed last year 500,000 copies of a guide book to the province. Good work was also done in New Brunswick. They had about 100,000 tourists and they estimated their revenue at 85,000,000. In order to show their interest in the tourist business I may say that the membership in the New Brunswick Tourist Association rose in one year from 800 to 1,400. Prince Edward Island also had
36,000	tourists last year and a revenue of $750,000 from that source. In Prince Edward Island the number of automobiles coming in. not owned on the island, was 800 in 1923 and 1,400 in 1924. I mention these facts simply to show that we in the Maritime provinces are alive to the importance of the tourist trade.

But there are things that we in the province cannot do. There is a limit to what we can do in the encouragement of the tourist trade, and it is right here that the federal government have an opportunity to do something for us if they will. There are two branches of the federal government which are connected directly or indirectly with the tourist trade; first, the National Parks branch, and second, the Natural Resources branch. The National Parks branch has charge of the national parks, of which we have ten, I believe, three in British Columbia, three in the prairie provinces, and four in Ontario. We in the Maritime provinces have no objection to those parks being there; we understand that that is probably the natural place for them. But the National Parks branch have also under their control historic sites and the marking of those historic sites by means of suitable monuments. What we would like in the Maritime provinces is this:	That
the National Parks branch take charge of the grounds at Fort Beausejour, for example; that they take charge of the grounds at Louisburg, and preserve them. They have already taken charge of a small area at Annapolis Royal. This is work that can only be done by the federal government, and we do not wish to duplicate in the provinces the departments that already exist at Ottawa. So it seems to me that there is work here for the National Parks branch. That department is doing good work up to the measure of their financial possibilities. We in this country, it seems to me, are lax in some respects, and one of these is the encouragement of such branches as the National Parks branch. We could have in New Brunswick a small national park, and we could have another in Nova Scotia, to add to our points of interest. In New Brunswick they have points of great scenic interest, such as the St. John valley, the valley of the Restigouche and the Mir-amichi. But what we require is simply that the federal government take hold of this thing when wre have carried it as far as we can. In Nova Scotia we have the Wentworth valley, the Annapolis valley and the Bras d'Or lakes-points of scenic cnterest. At some of these points a small national park could be located. The Natural Resources branch also in its work comes in contact directly and indirectly with the tourist trade. They examine into the natural resources of the country, follow out the waterways, outline canoe paths or trails, if you can call them such, and make maps. This is something that the provinces could hardly be expected to do. They should not be expected to duplicate the work that is being done or that

The Budget-Mr. Stansell
can be better done here at Ottawa. What we ask is that the federal government co-ordinate .the work of these branches, that they be given financial assistance so that they will be able to carry on the work, and that we should have here at Ottawa a tourist publicity bureau for the entire Dominion of Canada.
So far as the Maritime provinces are concerned, if we could get fair freight rates, increased marketing facilities, cold storage, and frost-proof warehouses, if we had wider markets and an increasing tourist trade, I believe that we would not suffer a great while in the province of Nova Scotia, at all events, under the present business depression.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel somewhat at a disadvantage at this late hour in endeavouring to offer a few remarks on the subject before the House. I do, however, wish to put before the House and the country my own personal views on this subject.
As far as the budget itself is concerned, there has been no criticism thus far so strong as that which has come from hon. members on the government side of the House. About thirty members supporting the government have already spoken, and almost without exception they have devoted themselves to every subject under the sun except the budget itself. The careful way in which they have avoided that subject is, I repeat, Mr. Speaker, the strongest condemnation that can be offered.
With the remarks of the speaker who has just preceded me (Mr. Robinson), I am very much in sympathy. I believe he has touched on a vital subject. I believe we possess in the natural resources of this Dominion, in our wonderful scenery and climate, a potential asset that can be developed and capitalized to a wonderful extent. However, while I sympathize very much with what the hon. member has just said, he like most of the other members on the government side has avoided nearly everything in the way of a reference to the budget itself.
We were treated this afternoon to a very long and eloquent address, which was also very much apart from the essentials of the budget. I had hoped, Mr. Speaker, that the wounds and sufferings of the war would not of necessity be drawn into this debate. The hon. member closed his address with a very eloquent appeal for national unity, for the elimination of all sectional strife and racial ill-feeling. His very eloquent appeal for unity followed an address which was nothing
if not an attempt to incite that very division he deplored. We were told something about the Ross rifle. The speaker himself claimed to know very little about this rifle. He also,
I believe, kept as far away from the actual use of it as possible, and he criticized strongly the men who shouldered that weapon and fought their country's battles in the bloodiest war of all history, carrying the weapons supplied to them, imposed on them, if you please, by the party of which he is a distinguished member. I have wondered, Mr. Speaker, how long in the constituency of the hon. member it will be necessary to manufacture campaign material of this type. Are there no great issues of the day that can be discussed? Is there nothing before us to-day on which an election can be won or lost that we have to revive the sores incidental to that fearful conflict? While it is very nice to discuss national unity and the elimination of all ill feeling, it seems to me it would be well to begin now to put in practice those high principles.
Since the beginning of this debate, compliments of various kinds have been handed to members of the cabinet and supporters of the government. I believe the Prime Minister himself can be complimented on the fact that he holds the record for a marathon performance in this fourteenth parliament, in delivering a speech over four hours in length. His record' has been nearly approached by other hon. members. I think this habit of making lengthy speeches is growing to too great an extent. The speeches might very well be condensed. The work of the House would be expedited, and the country itself would be very much better served by shorter and more practical speeches, by a little imore hard work and a little less talk.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) has been complimented on his sunny countenance and his transparent honesty.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) must be complimented on the amount of figures he has been able to put upon Hansard, but I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether the workmen of this country are not sufficiently intelligent to know whether they have a job or not. I wonder if industry in this country is not sufficiently intelligent to know whether it is working full time or not. I wonder whether all of us are not sufficiently intelligent to know whether we have money in our pockets and are prosperous or not. I do not intend to go into this in any further detail, because most of us know what the conditions of the country are. I think it is hardly
The Budget-Mr. Stansell

necessary for the Minister of Labour to supply page after page of statistics and figures to convince people of what they know already as to the conditions ctf to-day.
But to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) I think I can pay the most sincere compliment upon the brief way in which he delivered his budget statement. I can compliment him also on his ability in the art of juggling and sleight of hand. Perhaps this was necessary. An election cannot be so very far away, not more than about a year at the outside, and no doubt the government felt it was absolutely necessary to make a good showing and provide a surplus and, if possible, a reduction of debt. Therefore the minister accomplished, or set about to accomplish an impossibility, and the way in which that was attempted was certainly a credit to his ability. We have in this budget speech a statement of the country's finances, where figures are distributed through column after column with a sort of editorial comment. Looking at them one cannot but wonder at the deftness with which that distribution has been accomplished. Is it not time, Mr. Speaker, that a financial statement dealing with the affairs of the country should be presented in such a simple and practical way that the average man can understand just what the situation is? I ask you, would any company, any bank, or any organization dealing with the public that submits an annual statement, present the statement in the form in which this is given to us? There can only be one reason for a statement of this kind, it is intended to cover up the actual facts, to hide from the general public what the true situation is. I will not say this is the first time this has ever been attempted;
I do not propose to outline what anyone has done in former times. It is sufficient for me to deal with the facts as they are to-day; and I believe that the public of Canada, the electors who take an interest in the welfare of the country, are entitled to a simpler and plainer statement of the existing financial condition than they are getting. I believe, Sir, in the fair-mindedness of the public. I believe that the people of this country are willing to accept a plain statement of the facts, that they are willing to do their fair share in any way in which they may be called upon to remedy the condition that exists; and a first essential towards enlisting their sympathy and support is to give them a frank and open statement of the actual financial conditions of the country.
When changes were made in last year's budget an estimate was given that this would 
bring a reduction in revenue of about $24,000,000. We are told in this year's statement that that reduction was more than double; that . the actual reduction or falling off an revenue was $52,800,000. In the face of a decrease in revenue of $52,800,000, coupled with a greatly increased expenditure, the Acting Minister of Finance, if we accept his statement, is actually able to show that he has a very substantial surplus. This, I repeat, is a feat that very few would attempt and very few would succeed in accomplishing. I call attention to a statement made when this estimate was presented, in which it was predicted that there would be a reduction of $24,000,000. I quote the significant words which follow:
It is confidently expected that this reduction will give such impetus to trade that it will result in greater development of prosperity to all the provinces of Canada.
Now if prosperity is to come to any part of Canada, much less to all the provinces, I submit ilt must come in another form than this. The actual result is more than twice the amount the minister estimated. Therefore prosperity must be twice as great las he expected it to be. What a blessing, Mr. Speaker, it would be to this country, and) to all the provinces if based on that assumption the revenue had disappeared entirely. Certainly if the loss of $24,000,000 would bring prosperity, and by doubling that toss we would1 have even greater prosperity, then on the same assumption had we lost all our revenue we certainly would have reached! the millennium. I mention this to show the fallacy of the deductions dlrawn by the Acting Minister of Finance in his Statement.
Now, here is the statement by the hon. minister condensed. I use his own figures entirely, because we moist remember that the budget having been brought down early this session it was necessary to estimate some of the receipts and expenditures. I presume that no one is in a better position to estimate those amounts than the minister himself. I also presume that his canny Scotch caution would not allow him to exceed the expenditures very much or to reduce very much the revenues in his estimates. I therefore accept his figures in which he estimates the actual receipts at a total of $344,000,000. Against these the expenditures are estimated at $342,177,000, leaving a surplus of $1,823,000. As I said this is a somewhat complicated statement and in order to get at the facts it is necessary, if we take the minister's own figures, to do considerable figuring to arrive ait what we believe the true condition of affairs to be. I have spent some time working

The Budget-Mr. Stansell
on these figures, and I intend to submit what I think is the true and proper statement of the financial affairs of this country based on the figures supplied: by the minister himself. We have an actual revenue of $308,994,207.71. It is estimated by the minister that there is yet to be received $35,005,792.29, which makes $344,000,000 of total receipts. The expenditures, actual and estimated-and again I take the minister's own figures-are ais follows: Expenditures Actual and Estimated-
Ordinary	 $319,700,000
Capital	 18,077,000
Special	 4,400,000
Canadian National Railways	 18,027,000
Total	 $360,204,000
You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that I am not separating these amounts. It is true they are separated by the minister for purposes of his own; but I submit that the National Railways are owned by the people of Canada and any money advanced on their account is owed by the people and must be paid. Therefore in order to make this statement perfectly clear I am adding the amount of cash advanced to the railways, making a total expenditure of $360,204,000. Instead of there being a surplus there is an actual deficit of $16,204,000 and I submit, Mr. Speaker, this is the correct statement.
Now let us see what the railway financing is. It will be remembered that parliament authorized $56,527,000 for railway expenditure. This not being enough, a further supplementary estimate of $7,500,000 was approved, making a total of $64,027,000 divided as follows: Cash, $18,027,000; guaranteed bonds, $46,000,000. In addition to that there fell due Canadian Northern securities amounting to $17,000,000 which were Te-fmanced and for that reason are not counted. I merely mention this to show the amount of money required to finance our National Railway system. There was a further flotation issued by the railway itself of $9,375,000. This was for equipment and I presume the equipment was worth the money paid for it. I understand this loan was made by the railway system itself and was not specially guaranteed. We will therefore leave that out of consideration, because we take it for granted that the equipment was worth the money.
Then there was another special loan for the Toronto terminals, and branch lines, amounting to $18,000,000. This was guaranteed by the government. So that our total railway requirements for the year just past amounted to $10S,402,000. I mention this because there is a certain degree of pride on the part of the Canadian people in a railway that they own
and operate; but we must remember what that railway is costing the people, and when we hear people glibly talk about the reduction of freight rates and all such things as that, without taking into consideration that this will of necessity make that railway a greater white elephant on our hands than it is at present, it is well for us to pause and consider that we have spent during the year $108,402,000 on railway account. I will deduct from that securities that were re-financed on account of the Canadian Northern Railway, and also deduct the amount the railways issued for their own equipment. That leaves a balance of actual debt from the operation of the railways of $82,027,000. I will now give the figures supplied by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the increase of national debt. He figures the addition to
the public debt as follows:
Cash to Canadian National Railways.. .. $18,027,000 Canadian Government Merchant Marine.. ..	900,000
Quebec Harbour Commission	 600,000
That is an increase of $19,527,000, but he deducts from this a surplus which he showed in the first statement of $1,823,000. That will leave $17,704)300. But now he deducts something else; that is, an amount of $4,000,162, which is obtained in the following way. The governments of Greece and Roumania owe the Dominion and have owed the Dominion for some time a large sum of money which they have not repaid, nor have they paid interest on the money. The government have arranged for a funding of this amount of interest: that is, they have taken the amount of interest, of which not one dollar has been paid, and added it to the original amount, and then claimed this $4,000,162 was a surplus. It is just the same as though I held a mortgage on a man's farm so large that he was unable to pay a dollar of principal and had not paid any interest for some years, and I go to him and take a new mortgage, covering both principal and interest, and add the interest to the principal, and then say, "I have profited to the extent of the amount of interest added to the mortgage." If there is such a thing, Mr. Speaker, as unsound financing, this is an outstanding illustration. There may be something received in future years. We hope so, but no method of bookkeeping should show cash received before any cash has been received.
Reference is made in the budget to the fact that we now have added securities. I want to call attention to the fact that we had the security of the debtor, nations themselves before this, and we have not anything more than that now. You will notice

by this statement of figuring a fictitious surplus of $1,823,000 is added to another surplus of which we have never received a dollar, amounting to $4,000,162. Therefore, according to the statement of the minister the net increase in the national debt will only amount to $13,703,838. I propose now, to show what the actual increase of the national debt is. placing the statement on Hansard and then explaining how it is arrived at:

Again taking the minister's figures we are told that on March 31, 1924 the net public debt was $2,417,783,274.88; add on railway account, 1924-25, the sum of $82,027,000. It was pointed out by the minister that there was some difference between the cash advanced by the railways and the guaranteed bonds, but I must confess I am unable to understand where the difference is. In the one case we borrow the money on our own security and hand it over to the railways to the amount of $18,027,000. That is counted as a debt. In the other case we ask the railways to issue bonds for $46,000,000 and we guarantee them and they get the money. There is absolutely no difference. We, the people, are the railway. We own the railway. In the one case we have our own note, and in the other case we endorse the note of the railway and raise the money absolutely on the credit of the country. So that I say on railway account the debt is increased by $82,027,000. It cannot be disputed The people of Canada are just as much liable for that amount as they are for any other amount they have advanced. The railways have not repaid any money loaned them and are not likely to. There is no difference whether you advance money to a harbour commission, to other public works or to the railway,'because they are all owned iby Canada, and the debt incurred is money spent or money advanced by the people of Canada. There is no escape from it. Here is the situation: they add to the debt $S2,027,000. In addition there is a deficit, as I have shown, of $16,204,000, making a total addition to the debt for the past year of $98,231,000. That, Mr. Speaker, is a true financial statement of the affairs of this country and one which cannot be disputed.
It has been pointed out also by the minister that at the beginning of the year there were cash assets of over $43,000,000, and in order

to be accurate, I will read his statement to the House.
May I, before leaving this question of debt reduction, direct the attention of the House to the balance sheet of the Public Accounts at the close of the financial year 1923-24, page 2, where will be found among our assets an amount of $43,612,756.16, cash left in our hands after the closing of our accounts for that year; and I submit the question: Is not the actual possession of so much cash conclusive evidence that we ended that year with excellent results?
That is accounted for however by the fact that they borrowed the money and had not yet spent it. If that as a sound argument there should be a similar amount of cash on hand at the present time, but there is no reference in the minister's statement of any such amount of cash now.
Another matter to which I call attention is the statement made last year of the prosperity that would follow the reduction of taxation. You may look from one end of the statement to the other in this year's budget and will not find any such promise of the year that is to come. This is ample proof that the financial statement might even be worse than I have outlined, but the figures I have given are those taken from the minister's own report and I submit they are correct.
A great deal has been said about the policy of the government. I do not want to be unduly harsh and I am going to state frankly that I do not think all the unemployment and all the difficulties with which we are faced are due to the government, but I do think that they did their very best to bring about this condition. They have not done a great deal in the past four years, but in my humble judgment everything that has been done has been wrong, and I will attempt to prove that that is so. I do not claim for one moment that the immediate adoption of a Conservative policy or the proper application of adequate protection will at once restore prosperity, but I believe it will materially assist in that direction, and the sooner those policies are applied1 the sooner the remedy will come.
A discussion of policies present and prospective brings us to that old somewhat threadbare subject, the tariff, protection versus free trade. Undoubtedly many beautiful arguments can be submitted by those who sincerely believe in free trade. Many of those arguments are founded on a study of the theories of Cobden, Bright, Henry George and others. I should like to point out that this whole thing is based on a theory intended to apply to conditions that never existed in this world and in my judgment will not exist within a generation at least, if ever. The benefits of such a policy as free trade could be real only to the extent to which all

The Budget-Mr. Stansell
nations adopted the same policy. This theory of free trade, however beautiful it may be, is absolutely worthless and impracticable as applied to -conditions as they exist to-day. I am quite sure there are only a very few members in this House who really and honestly believe in their hearts that free trade is the proper thing for Canada. Fortunately, they are very few, and to such I can only offer sympathy because I am convinced that there is no practical method by which free trade can be applied with beneficial results to the Dominion of Canada at the present time. We are faced with conditions and facts, not with theories.
Briefly, what are conditions in Canada today? We have taken our share in a war that, in magnitude, in expenditure of men and money, in its fearful results, has never before been equalled in the world. It is folly to think that Canada or any of the allies, or, indeed, any nation even most remotely connected with the war, can go through such a period without tremendous commercial disturbances. During the period of the war, business was stimulated to a wonderful degree, advanced and enlarged, spending habits were contracted, the people were spending and reducing their own buying power, so that at the close of the conflict a reaction was inevitable. The only thing that could or should have occurred was a realization of the results that must come from such a conflict and the proper application of remedies which, although they might not be entirely curative, would at least have been preventive. Many nations of the world, amongst others the United States, realizing that, used the only weapon which they had to work with-a protective tariff. Sixty-five nations have increased their tariff since the war with the direct object of trying to conserve and protect their own resources to supply within themselves the limited buying power of their people. Canada, through a mistaken policy, is perhaps the one outstanding nation which took the opposite course, with the result that most of us know. I said a short time ago that the only thing that this government has done has been a mistaken act. The little that it has done has been in the wrong direction. While I never was a believer in high protection, I am convinced that from the standpoint of the farmer, labouring man. manufacturer or anyone else in this Dominion, we should at once, faced with that condition, have revised our tariff and made it so as to fit conditions as they were. <
This is the condition that faces us. Our buying power is reduced. The buying power of all
the nations of the world is reduced. They are buying only the things they must, of necessity, buy. There can be only one result.
We must curtail our expenditure,
11 ip.m. reduce many of our activities and live, as far as possible, within ourselves. Surely, when buying power is low. when men are out of jobs, it is not a practical policy to go to a foreign nation and buy goods that we could produce ourselves. I do not propose to deal with the tariff as it affects a particular individual or class. I contend that whatever policy we put into force should be one for the general benefit of Canada.
In addition to conditions which I have described, we have a system of national railways besides the great railway system of the Canadian Pacific. These, with their branch lines, form three great lines, running east and west across this country. That is, the money of the people of Canada is invested in railway lines running east and west. With the enormous debt that that entails, there are created fixed charges which must be met by the people of the Dominion and the only way in which those fixed charges can be reduced and the railway deficits removed is to keep those railways busy. We have a tremendous national debt which, as I have shown, amounts to about $2,500,000,000, which also involves an enormous fixed charge in the way of interest. The only method by which that can be carried by the people of this Dominion without an undue burden is to enlarge and invigorate our commercial interests in Canada, to increase the volume of business that is done. Any other system is bound to be ruinous. With conditions such as these, with our money invested in railways and with our tremendous national debt, both of which entail enormous fixed charges against us, the only way in which we can get out of such a situation is to reduce overhead so that we can carry the burden without its resting too heavily upon us. To do this we must have increased population and employment for our people, and our farmers and employees in our factories must be producing sufficient to carry the load.
Another reason why a protective tariff is absolutely essential to the Dominion is this. For 3,000 miles we are alongside a neighbour upon which, whether we like it or not, we are dependent for certain conditions. A certain scale of wages is in effect over there, for example, the McAdoo award in regard to wages of railway employees, and whether we
The Budget-Mr. Stansell

like it or not we are forced to accept the same scale of wages in Canada. If not, if wages are lower on any particular line in Canada than they are on the corresponding line in the United States, it is very easy for our workers to walk across the border, and with the conditions that we have had during the last few years that is just what has happened, to the great detriment of this country, We deliberately adopted the policy which encouraged greater importations from the United States, with the result that our workmen have had to go over there to get a job. This is axiomatic,. I think, and incontrovertible: whereever the nation sends its money, there its sons and daughters are bound to go. This is inevitable. If our money goes to the United States or to any other country to build up industries there, your sons and daughters must go there to get work. There is no escape from it. It may not be pleasant, but it is true nevertheless. As an illustration, I might mention something that was made a great deal of some years ago when the Farmers' party first had its rise, although I do not hear 60 much about it to-day, and I rather think the idea has been exploded-a great deal was said about the depopulation of the farms and the rural people drifting into the large urban centres. Years ago when there was a far greater proportion of our population in the country, a great many of our farmers were obliged to meet their requirements by their own handiwork, and what they failed in so supplying they obtained from the comer store, their money being spent at home as far as possible. To-day how many farm houses will you go into throughout Ontario and Quebec where you will not find Eaton's or Simpson's catalogue in a prominent place? The people are sending their money to Toronto and the other big centres to furnish their requirements. I am not finding fault with this but again my axiom applies:	If your money goes to any
of these large centres, your sons and daughters must go there to get their living and in an even greater degree, the same holds true when we send our money to a foreign country.
Now, as I said, we are dependent on the United States, in that whatever fiscal system they adopt we are forced1 in self defence to adopt something similar, otherwise ruin stares us in the face. Now, does anyone think that, forced as we are to pay wages on the same scale that obtains in the United States, we can manufacture goods to compete with the cheap labour of Europe? We cannot do so. With our high overhead, therefore, we need protection from cheap foreign labour to hold our own. Now, as I said, the government in

my judgment adopted an entirely wrong policy at a most critical time in the history of Canada. When the national sickness was acute they neglected their patient, at the very time when a stimulant should have been administered they resorted to bleeding. Why, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friends from the west and also some of their party from Ontario-I believe they are entirely sincere-conceived the idea that because something was wrong with the body politic it must be the tariff, and that therefore it should be done away with. They demanded free trade, and because their platform coincided almost word' for word with the one adopted by the Liberal party before they came into power, in order to secure sufficient votes to continue in office the government went a little way -and I think against their better judgment- in the reduction of the tariff. This has resulted in the closing down of factories, unemployment, emigration to the United States, and a loss of revenue to the tune of $52,800,000. I should like to know whether one man or one class has received any benefit from that policy. I know the whip of the Progressive party (Mr. Johnston) said that the agricultural people had. That is a business which I know a great deal about for I was raised on the farm and have farmed all my life, consequently I am familiar with the purchase of agricultural implements and of all other things necessary to equip a farm. I remember that about twenty-five years ago when the duty on agricultural implements was 20 per cent we had the cheapest implements in the history of the country. I do not say that the tariff was the only reason for their cheapness. My point is that the application of a customs tariff does not always increase the price to the consumer of the article protected, and I think it is very easy for hon. members to prove that to their own satisfaction. When a high duty was imposed on our cattle by the United States tariff, where did the complaint come fiom? It came from our western farmers who desired to ship their cattle across the line, and they complained that they were shut out from the American market. It was true; we were the ones that suffered, not the consumers in the United States. Now we had a most substantial reduction in the tariff on agricultural implements. What was the result? In order to enable the implement makers to break even they were given their raw material practically free of duty, with the result that the factories that supplied that raw material are to-day out of business or working half time. The result to them has been disastrous. Now, who benefited? Figures have been given, and no one disputed them, that the price of

The Budget-Mr. Stansell
agricultural implements, save for the reduction of the sales tax-and even then the full amount was not given-has not been decreased.

That reduction represents just exactly the sales tax and no more, and in the case, just cited, of twelve implements with reduction of $57 the same is true. I am not speaking of the removal of the sales tax. I say that the reduced price of farm implements due to the reduction of the tariff has not materialized, and therefore the farmer has not benefited. But even if it had materialized, there is another article of manufacture which in my family represents a substantial expenditure, that is boots and shoes. Some hon. members desired a reduced tariff on boots and shoes; they did not get it; there was a reduction of the sales tax I believe. There is a very high duty on boots and shoes compared to implements, but what I am concerned about is the actual price paid by the purchaser of these goods when he goes to the retail store. I have found by actual experience that I am buying boots and shoes at a greater proportionate reduction now than I am buying agricultural implements at, and yet the customs tariff has not been reduced. I find by a study of Eaton's spring catalogues for 1924 and 1925- and I think
most hon. members will agree that this is pretty good authority-I find that on about half a dozen lines, such as Shoes for men, boots for lumbermen and labouring men, and ladies' shoes, there is a reduction in the prices I am paying of from 11 to 16 per cent, and the same holds true in the retail stores. So that substantially the consumer has enjoyed a greater advantage in the reduction of the price of boots and shoes, on which there was no reduction of tariff, than he has received in respect of agricultural implements, on which the tariff is nearly all taken away. In addition to that, as I have said, manufacturers of raw material have suffered very seriously.
Another thing we have heard a great deal about is fertilizer, concerning which figures were given the other night. It had been shown that there was a widespread demand that fertilizer be placed on the free list, and when action was taken in response to that demand the result was that most of the factories ceased operation, and if I wished to buy fertilizer this year I would pay more for it than I did a year ago. Again I say, who got any benefit? The country lost $52,000,000 in revenue; the labourer lost his job; the capital invested in industry was either greatly depreciated or lost and no one got any substantial benefit.
Some statements were made to-night by the hon. member for North Huron (Mr. King), to which I wish at this stage to make reference. I give the hon. gentleman credit for presenting figures that were correct; I have no reason to dispute them. I also give him credit for being absolutely sincere in the deductions he drew from those figures. But in my judgment, and I am sure in the judgment of this House, he was entirely wrong in his conclusions. The figures had reference to the comparative protection in Canada and the United States, and he showed that Canada was very much more highly protected than the United States because Canada collected more per capita in customs taxation than the United States did. Well, the facts are so clear that I am surprised that the hon. member did not understand the situation. I will try to point out what the real condition is. In many lines of goods the United States tariff is twice or three times as high as ours, so high that it is almost prohibitive and outside1 goods are largely shut out; therefore the people of the United States buy home manufactured goods. If that is a desirable condition, then I say let us try the same thing in Canada.

speechtext:
How do they collect such a large amount of duty if the goods are shut out?
The Budget-Mr. Stansell

Goods are not entirely shut out (because they certainly collect quite a lot, but if their tariff was higher they would collect less. The fact remains that they collect less than we do per capita because they have their tariff so high that it shuts out very many lines. I do not say it shuts out everything, but it keeps out so much that they are not paying as much as we are per capita in customs duties. Our tariff is so low that we are being encouraged to 'buy from foreign countries. The result is that in the last ten years we have had an unfavourable trade balance with the United States amounting to about $2,000,000,000. I know it is a favourite argument of hon. gentlemen to my left

and they are perfectly sincere-that if you sell you must buy; that there must be international1 trade. That is true, but it does not mean that you must buy things that you can produce at home. If a farmer operated on such a system as that there would only be one place for him and that is the poor house. Let me point out that you can buy a bank balance; you can buy life insurance; you can buy a competence for old age, just as you can buy potatoes, eggs, butter and other things of that kind. It is the part of wisdom for every farmer to sell those things that he can produce and sell at a profit and to buy only those things that he cannot advantageously produce himself, and, as far as possible, to secure for himself some of the comforts in the way of insurance, a competency for old age or a bank balance.
What have we been doing in respect to our trade with the United States? We have had an adverse balance of $2,000,000,000 in ten years; what have we done to offset that? We have gone over there and borrowed money. Had we not followed that system of borrowing money our dollar would be very much below par to-day. The borrowing carried out by the Minister of Finance on the New York market did much to stabilize the value of the dollar, but it does not justify our purchasing in the United States goods that we could produce at home, nor does it justify an adverse trade balance with the United States from year to year. So long as we do that we are encouraging the United States to take a mortgage on Canada's future to the extent to which we allow that adverse trade balance to accrue.
I know that to some the word " protection " has a disagreeable sound. But protection is a very good thing when it is applied to insurance against fire; it is a very good thing as applied to the home. It costs something, but we think we should have it. National

protection is just as vital to the nation as home protection is to the home, and the quicker we Canadians realize this and institute a proper national policy, the better it will be for us. We do not believe that adequate protection can do everything; there are many other factors that must be taken into consideration. But we must view all these questions in a national way. We must practise some real national unity instead of just talking about it; and one of the first essentials is so to protect ourselves that so far as possible we can supply our own labourers with a job and not force them to go to the United States to get the employment they should get" here.
Somebody will ask me right away, how can protection be of any benefit to the farmer? Well, I am advocating it, and I am a farmer; I think it is of some benefit. I will admit for the sake of argument that it may not appeal quite so much to the western farmers as it does to the farmers of Ontario. But should Canada's immigration increase, her population be augmented and her factories start to operate at full time as the result of the application of sound policies, I will trust the farmers of Ontario and of Canada as a whole to get their share of that prosperity. Anyone who thinks that the general enhanced prosperity will be of no 'benefit to the farmer is sadly mistaken. When the men have employment, when the factories are running full time; when development has taken place in our mines and our other resources, a buying power is created; a market is opened up for milk, cheese, butter, eggs, wheat and everything the farmer produces, and there will be no doubt, about whether such a condition will benefit the farmer.
I am sorry the horn, member for North Huron (Mr. King) was not in his seat when I was answering his argument about customs duties in Canada and the United States. At the risk of repetition I should just like to make the point again. He said that protection was higher in Canada than in the United States because less was collected in the United States by way of customs duties than in Canada.

He said that five or seven cattle, I forget the exact number, had been sold for $57. The man who shipped first-class cattle, in spite of the fact that conditions are not as good as we would like to see them, received a good return. The other man shipped half a dozen cattle and got about $10 apiece for them. I never saw the cattle in question, but they could not have been fit for market or they would 'have brought more money. There ds one lesson to be drawn from this. Just as our manufacturers, if they want to get a good price, must produce good goods, so the farmers, if they want to get a good price for their cattle or their butter or any other of their products, must produce a good article. While prices are not as high as I would like to see them, I believe that the farmer has passed the worst turn, and that things are bound to improve a little bit from the farmer's standpoint. Conditions are not so bad after all when we find prices like this being paid. This is not a specially prepared case, but is just an ordinary statement referring to Alberta cattle shipped and sold on the St. Boniface market.
The. Budget-Mr. Gendron

Therefore the one thing necessary is for us to adopt a policy of Canada first. Surely it is our duty to look after our own nation, rather than look after the American nation or any other nation in the world, and until we do, Canada will not have the prosperity that she is entitled to and that she needs. I do not admit for one moment that an increase of customs tariff must mean an increase in the price. What we do want is a job for our workmen and lower costs, but we shall never get that happy result if we always send to some other country for the things we might very well produce at home. Let us as members of this House and as citizens of this great country, with the resources^ we hear so much about, forget some of the little things and get busy on a national policy, practise national economy, and work for national unity.
I sympathize very much with the aims of hon. members to my left, and I was glad to hear the prophecy of the hon. member to whom I have just referred as to the length of time the Progressive party will live. I hope it will live a great length of time, and that its present leader will lead it providing he adopts a sound fiscal policy, for I believe he is sincere. Undoubtedly the hon. member for Brandon honestly desires the welfare of all Canada but he is on the wrong track, the policies he would like to put in force are mistaken ones; and I would urge him and his followers to consider seriously this question in the light of national necessities, and see if there is not something else that the Dominion of Canada wants at the present time rather than a reduction of the tariff. I have a high opinion of the party to my left and of their leader, but they are mistaken in their policies, I firmly believe. They are riding on a political New York Central and are travelling in a circle. Let them all get on the Canadian National line and get somewhere.
